F3.3  CONSTANT, CONSTANT-MULTIPLE AND SUM RULES
B. d/dx [c] = 0
   d/dx [c f(x)] = c f'(x)
   d/dx [f(x) + g(x)] = f'(x) + g'(x)        (and for differences)
C. SYMBOLS: c a constant; f, g differentiable functions.
D. CONCEPT: differentiation is LINEAR: it acts term by term and pulls out
   constants.
E. CONDITIONS: f and g differentiable at x.
F. DERIVATION: from the limit laws (F2.2), since the difference quotient
   of f+g is the sum of the difference quotients.
G. EXAMPLE: d/dx [5x^3 - 4x + 7] = 15x^2 - 4.
H. INTERPRETATION: derivatives of sums and multiples are computed term
   by term: differentiation is a linear operator.
I. MISTAKE: the product and quotient are NOT term-by-term: (fg)' !=
   f'g'.
J. RELATED: linearity of integration (F4.3) and of expectation (F36.2).

F3.4  POWER RULE
A. NAME: Power rule.
B. FORMULA:   d/dx [ x^n ] = n x^(n-1)
C. SYMBOLS: n is any real constant (integer, negative, fraction); x the
   variable (x > 0 or such that x^n is defined/differentiable).
D. CONCEPT: the slope of x^n at x is n times the "one lower power". For
   n=2: the curve x^2 at x has slope 2x: steeper the further out.
   Why: when x grows by h, x^n changes by about n x^(n-1) h
   (one of the n factors changes, n ways to choose which).
E. CONDITIONS: the variable is in the BASE and the exponent is a
   CONSTANT. For a CONSTANT base and variable exponent (2^x) the
   power rule does NOT apply (use F3.8). For x^x neither applies (use
   logarithmic differentiation, F3.9).
F. DERIVATION for positive integer n (binomial theorem F1.7):
     (x + h)^n = x^n + n x^(n-1) h + C(n,2) x^(n-2) h^2 + ...
     ( (x+h)^n - x^n ) / h = n x^(n-1) + (terms with h) -> n x^(n-1).
G. EXAMPLES
   Simple: d/dx x^5 = 5x^4;  d/dx sqrt(x) = d/dx x^(1/2)
           = (1/2) x^(-1/2) = 1/(2 sqrt(x));  d/dx (1/x^3)
           = d/dx x^(-3) = -3 x^(-4) = -3/x^4.
   Moderate: f(x) = 4 x^(3/2) - 6/x + 2 sqrt(x) at x = 4.
        Rewrite: 4x^(3/2) - 6x^(-1) + 2x^(1/2).
        f'(x) = 6 x^(1/2) + 6 x^(-2) + x^(-1/2).
        At x = 4: 6*2 + 6/16 + 1/2 = 12 + 0.375 + 0.5 = 12.875.
H. INTERPRETATION: the sign and size of 12.875 say f is rising steeply
   at x = 4: increasing x by 0.01 raises f by about 0.129.
I. MISTAKES: bringing the exponent down but forgetting to subtract 1;
   differentiating 1/x^3 as 1/(3x^2); using the power rule on 2^x.
J. RELATED: chain rule extends it to (g(x))^n.

F3.5  PRODUCT RULE
B. FORMULA: d/dx [ f(x) g(x) ] = f'(x) g(x) + f(x) g'(x)
C. SYMBOLS: f, g differentiable; f' and g' their derivatives.
D. CONCEPT: a rectangle with sides f and g has area fg. When both sides
   change a little, the area change is (change in f)*g + f*(change in
   g) + a negligible corner term of order (change)^2. Dividing by dx
   gives the rule.
E. CONDITIONS: both differentiable. NOT (fg)' = f'g'.
F. DERIVATION:
     f(x+h)g(x+h) - f(x)g(x)
       = [f(x+h) - f(x)] g(x+h) + f(x) [g(x+h) - g(x)]
   Divide by h; as h -> 0, g(x+h) -> g(x) (continuity).
G. EXAMPLES
   Simple: d/dx [x^2 e^x] = 2x e^x + x^2 e^x = e^x (x^2 + 2x).
   Moderate: d/dx [ (3x + 1) ln x ] = 3 ln x + (3x + 1)/x
           = 3 ln x + 3 + 1/x.
H. INTERPRETATION: sensitivity of a product splits into the two
   contributions.
I. MISTAKE: (fg)' = f'g'. Forgetting one of the two terms.
J. RELATED: quotient rule is the product rule with 1/g.

blocks.title: DERIVATIVE TABLE (memorize; each derived from the rules)
blocks.formulaBody:
d/dx e^x       = e^x
     d/dx a^x       = a^x ln a                    (a > 0)
     d/dx ln x      = 1/x                          (x > 0)
     d/dx ln|x|     = 1/x                          (x != 0)
     d/dx log_a x   = 1/(x ln a)
     d/dx sin x     = cos x
     d/dx cos x     = -sin x
     d/dx tan x     = sec^2 x = 1/cos^2 x
     d/dx arctan x  = 1/(1 + x^2)
     d/dx sqrt(x)   = 1/(2 sqrt(x))
     d/dx 1/x       = -1/x^2
   Chain-rule versions:
     d/dx e^(g(x)) = g'(x) e^(g(x));   d/dx ln(g(x)) = g'(x)/g(x).

d/dx e^x       = e^x

   Chain-rule versions:

parts.C: SYMBOLS: trig functions use RADIANS.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: e^x is its own derivative: the growth rate of e^x equals its
   current size (definition of "natural" exponential growth).
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: ln x and 1/x need x > 0 (or x != 0); a^x needs a > 0;
   trigonometric derivatives assume radians; tan x needs cos x != 0.
parts.F:
DERIVATION of d/dx e^x: (e^(x+h) - e^x)/h = e^x (e^h - 1)/h -> e^x * 1
   using lim (e^h - 1)/h = 1 (F2.4).
   d/dx ln x: if y = ln x then e^y = x; differentiate implicitly:
   e^y y' = 1 -> y' = 1/e^y = 1/x.
   d/dx a^x: a^x = e^(x ln a), chain rule gives ln a * e^(x ln a).
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: d/dx 5e^(3x) = 15 e^(3x).  d/dx ln(2x) = 2/(2x) = 1/x.
   Moderate: d/dx [ ln(x^2 + 4x) ] = (2x + 4)/(x^2 + 4x) at x = 2:
        (8)/(12) = 2/3.
   Moderate 2: d/dx [x * ln x - x] = ln x + 1 - 1 = ln x. (So
        x ln x - x is an antiderivative of ln x; Module 4.)
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: e^x is the only function (up to a constant multiple)
   equal to its own derivative; ln x has slope 1/x (slope 1 at x = 1).
parts.J:
RELATED: logistic regression derivative; log-likelihood gradients
   (Module 38); softmax.

blocks.title: LOGARITHMIC DIFFERENTIATION
blocks.formulaBody:
If y = f(x)^(g(x)) or a long product/quotient: take ln of both sides,
   differentiate implicitly:
       ln y = g(x) ln f(x)    =>   y'/y = ( g(x) ln f(x) )'
       y' = y * ( g(x) ln f(x) )'.

parts.B:
If y = f(x)^(g(x)) or a long product/quotient: take ln of both sides,
   differentiate implicitly:
       ln y = g(x) ln f(x)    =>   y'/y = ( g(x) ln f(x) )'
       y' = y * ( g(x) ln f(x) )'.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: logs turn powers and products into sums that are easy to
   differentiate.
parts.E: CONDITIONS: f(x) > 0 (or use |f|).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: y'/y is the relative (percentage) rate of change, so
   products become sums of relative rates.
parts.I: MISTAKE: using the power rule (x^x)' = x * x^(x-1).
parts.J:
RELATED: log-likelihood differentiates sums, not products, for the
   same reason (Module 38).

F3.9  LOGARITHMIC DIFFERENTIATION
B. If y = f(x)^(g(x)) or a long product/quotient: take ln of both sides,

       y' = y * ( g(x) ln f(x) )'.
C. SYMBOLS: y the function; f(x) > 0 the base and g(x) the exponent;
   y'/y = (ln y)' is the logarithmic derivative (relative rate of
   change).
D. CONCEPT: logs turn powers and products into sums that are easy to
   differentiate.
E. CONDITIONS: f(x) > 0 (or use |f|).
G. EXAMPLES: y = x^x (x > 0). ln y = x ln x; y'/y = ln x + 1;
   y' = x^x (ln x + 1). At x = 1: y = 1, y' = 1*(0 + 1) = 1.
   Moderate: y = x^2 (x+1)^3 / (2x - 1)^4. ln y = 2 ln x + 3 ln(x+1)
   - 4 ln(2x-1);  y'/y = 2/x + 3/(x+1) - 8/(2x-1).
H. INTERPRETATION: y'/y is the relative (percentage) rate of change, so
   products become sums of relative rates.
I. MISTAKE: using the power rule (x^x)' = x * x^(x-1).
J. RELATED: log-likelihood differentiates sums, not products, for the
   same reason (Module 38).

J. RELATED: logistic regression derivative; log-likelihood gradients
   (Module 38); softmax.

F3.9  LOGARITHMIC DIFFERENTIATION
B. If y = f(x)^(g(x)) or a long product/quotient: take ln of both sides,
   differentiate implicitly:
       ln y = g(x) ln f(x)    =>   y'/y = ( g(x) ln f(x) )'
       y' = y * ( g(x) ln f(x) )'.
C. SYMBOLS: y the function; f(x) > 0 the base and g(x) the exponent;
   y'/y = (ln y)' is the logarithmic derivative (relative rate of
   change).
D. CONCEPT: logs turn powers and products into sums that are easy to
   differentiate.
E. CONDITIONS: f(x) > 0 (or use |f|).
G. EXAMPLES: y = x^x (x > 0). ln y = x ln x; y'/y = ln x + 1;
   y' = x^x (ln x + 1). At x = 1: y = 1, y' = 1*(0 + 1) = 1.
   Moderate: y = x^2 (x+1)^3 / (2x - 1)^4. ln y = 2 ln x + 3 ln(x+1)
   - 4 ln(2x-1);  y'/y = 2/x + 3/(x+1) - 8/(2x-1).
H. INTERPRETATION: y'/y is the relative (percentage) rate of change, so
   products become sums of relative rates.
I. MISTAKE: using the power rule (x^x)' = x * x^(x-1).
J. RELATED: log-likelihood differentiates sums, not products, for the
   same reason (Module 38).

sections.title: IMPLICIT DIFFERENTIATION

blocks.title: IMPLICIT DIFFERENTIATION
blocks.formulaBody:
PROCEDURE: for a relation F(x, y) = 0 that defines y as a
   (local) function of x:
     1. Differentiate both sides with respect to x, treating y as y(x)
        so that d/dx [y^n] = n y^(n-1) * y'  (chain rule).
     2. Collect all terms with y' on one side.
     3. Solve for y'.

parts.B:
PROCEDURE: for a relation F(x, y) = 0 that defines y as a
   (local) function of x:
     1. Differentiate both sides with respect to x, treating y as y(x)
        so that d/dx [y^n] = n y^(n-1) * y'  (chain rule).
     2. Collect all terms with y' on one side.
     3. Solve for y'.
parts.C: SYMBOLS: y' = dy/dx.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: some curves (circles) cannot be written y = f(x) globally,
   but they still have a well-defined slope at most points.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: slope formula usually has y in the denominator; it fails
   (vertical tangent) where that denominator is 0.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: x^2 + y^2 = 25. 2x + 2y y' = 0 -> y' = -x/y.
        At (3, 4): y' = -3/4. Tangent: y - 4 = -(3/4)(x - 3).
        The slope is perpendicular to the radius (slope 4/3): product
        -1. OK.
   Moderate: Folium x^3 + y^3 = 6xy at (3, 3). (Check: 27 + 27 = 54 =
        6*9. OK.)
        3x^2 + 3y^2 y' = 6y + 6x y'
        y' (3y^2 - 6x) = 6y - 3x^2
        y' = (2y - x^2)/(y^2 - 2x).
        At (3,3): (6 - 9)/(9 - 6) = -1.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: the slope -x/y of x^2 + y^2 = 25 is the negative
   reciprocal of the radius slope y/x: the tangent is perpendicular to
   the radius.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: forgetting y' when differentiating a y term; dividing by
   zero at points of vertical tangent.
parts.J:
RELATED: related rates; implicit function theorem (supplementary);
   level curves (Module 12): the gradient is normal to F(x,y) = c.

sections.title: FIRST AND SECOND DERIVATIVES; INCREASING AND DECREASING FUNCTIONS

blocks.title: MONOTONICITY TEST (FIRST-DERIVATIVE TEST FOR INCREASE/DECREASE)
blocks.formulaBody:
On an interval I:
     f'(x) > 0 for all x in I  =>  f is increasing on I.
     f'(x) < 0 for all x in I  =>  f is decreasing on I.
     f'(x) = 0 for all x in I  =>  f is constant on I.

parts.B:
On an interval I:
     f'(x) > 0 for all x in I  =>  f is increasing on I.
     f'(x) < 0 for all x in I  =>  f is decreasing on I.
     f'(x) = 0 for all x in I  =>  f is constant on I.
parts.C: SYMBOLS: "increasing" means x1 < x2 implies f(x1) < f(x2).
parts.D: CONCEPT: positive slope = going uphill.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: f continuous on I and differentiable inside. (The test
   gives a sufficient, not necessary, condition: f(x) = x^3 is
   increasing even though f'(0) = 0.)
parts.G:
EXAMPLES: f(x) = x^3 - 3x: f'(x) = 3(x^2 - 1) is positive for |x| > 1
   (increasing on (-inf, -1) and (1, inf)) and negative on (-1, 1)
   (decreasing). f(x) = x^3 is increasing although f'(0) = 0.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: the sign of the derivative gives the direction of
   change; a loss decreases along directions where its derivative is
   negative.
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: requiring f' > 0 everywhere for 'increasing'
   (isolated zeros are fine); testing the sign at one point instead of
   on the whole interval.
parts.J: RELATED: critical points (F3.12), gradient descent (F43.2).

blocks.title: CRITICAL POINTS AND THE FIRST-DERIVATIVE TEST
blocks.formulaBody:
A CRITICAL POINT of f is a point c in the domain where f'(c) = 0 or
   f'(c) does not exist. Candidates for local extrema occur only at
   critical points (Fermat's theorem: if f has a local extremum at an
   interior point c where f is differentiable, then f'(c) = 0).
   First-derivative test at a critical point c:
     f' changes + to - at c  => local maximum.
     f' changes - to + at c  => local minimum.
     f' does not change sign => no local extremum (e.g. x^3 at 0).

parts.B:
A CRITICAL POINT of f is a point c in the domain where f'(c) = 0 or
   f'(c) does not exist. Candidates for local extrema occur only at
   critical points (Fermat's theorem: if f has a local extremum at an
   interior point c where f is differentiable, then f'(c) = 0).
   First-derivative test at a critical point c:
     f' changes + to - at c  => local maximum.
     f' changes - to + at c  => local minimum.
     f' does not change sign => no local extremum (e.g. x^3 at 0).
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: c a critical point; f'(c) the derivative there; the sign
   pattern of f' just left and right of c decides the type.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: at a smooth peak or valley the tangent is horizontal
   (Fermat); a sign change of f' from + to - marks a peak, from - to + a
   valley.
parts.E: !! WARNING !! f'(c) = 0 does NOT guarantee an extremum.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES: f(x) = x^3 - 3x + 1: f' = 3(x - 1)(x + 1): + to - at x = -1
   (local max, f = 3), - to + at x = 1 (local min, f = -1). f(x) = x^3:
   f'(0) = 0 but no sign change, so no extremum. f(x) = |x|: f'(0) does
   not exist; x = 0 is the global minimum.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: critical points are the only candidates for interior
   extrema.
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: assuming f'(c) = 0 means an extremum; forgetting
   points where f' does not exist; ignoring endpoints.
parts.J:
RELATED: second-derivative test (F3.14), closed-interval method
   (F3.13), gradient equal to zero (F43.2).

sections.title: LOCAL AND GLOBAL (ABSOLUTE) MAXIMA AND MINIMA

blocks.rawText:
DEFINITIONS
  Local (relative) maximum at c: f(c) >= f(x) for all x NEAR c.
  Global (absolute) maximum at c: f(c) >= f(x) for ALL x in the domain.
  Similarly for minima.
  A global extremum is also a local one, but not conversely.

blocks.title: CLOSED-INTERVAL METHOD (for global extrema on [a, b])
blocks.formulaBody:
For f continuous on [a, b]:
     1. Find all critical points in (a, b).
     2. Evaluate f at the critical points AND at the endpoints a and b.
     3. Largest value = global max; smallest = global min.

parts.B:
For f continuous on [a, b]:
     1. Find all critical points in (a, b).
     2. Evaluate f at the critical points AND at the endpoints a and b.
     3. Largest value = global max; smallest = global min.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: [a, b] the interval; c the critical points inside it; f(a),
   f(b) the endpoint values.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: a continuous function on a closed interval must attain its
   extremes (EVT), and they occur at critical points or endpoints, so
   only finitely many values need comparing.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: continuity on a closed bounded interval guarantees
   existence (EVT, F2.7). On an open or unbounded domain extremes may not
   exist; study limits at the ends.
parts.G:
EXAMPLE: f(x) = x^3 - 3x + 1 on [-2, 3].
     f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 = 0 -> x = -1 or 1.
     f(-2) = -8 + 6 + 1 = -1;  f(-1) = -1 + 3 + 1 = 3;
     f(1) = 1 - 3 + 1 = -1;    f(3) = 27 - 9 + 1 = 19.
     Global max = 19 at x = 3; global min = -1 at x = -2 and x = 1.
     Local max at x = -1 (value 3), local min at x = 1 (value -1).
G2 (APPLIED): fence 200 m to enclose a rectangle. Width x, length
     100 - x. Area A(x) = x(100 - x) on [0, 100]. A'(x) = 100 - 2x = 0
     -> x = 50. A(0) = 0, A(50) = 2500, A(100) = 0. Maximum 2500 m^2
     (a square).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: the largest candidate value is the global maximum,
   the smallest the global minimum.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: forgetting endpoints; not checking that the critical point
   is inside the interval.
parts.J:
RELATED: extreme value theorem (F2.7), optimization over bounded sets
   (Module 43).

sections.title: CONCAVITY AND INFLECTION POINTS

blocks.title: SECOND DERIVATIVE, CONCAVITY, SECOND-DERIVATIVE TEST
blocks.formulaBody:
/RULES
     f''(x) = d/dx [ f'(x) ]   (second derivative; also d^2 f/dx^2)
     f'' > 0 on I  => f is CONCAVE UP (convex, "cup", slope increasing)
     f'' < 0 on I  => f is CONCAVE DOWN ("cap", slope decreasing)
     Inflection point: a point where concavity changes (f'' changes
     sign); at such a point f'' = 0 or does not exist (necessary, not
     sufficient).
     SECOND-DERIVATIVE TEST: if f'(c) = 0 then
       f''(c) > 0 => local minimum at c
       f''(c) < 0 => local maximum at c
       f''(c) = 0 => test inconclusive (use the first-derivative test).

parts.B:
FORMULA/RULES
     f''(x) = d/dx [ f'(x) ]   (second derivative; also d^2 f/dx^2)
     f'' > 0 on I  => f is CONCAVE UP (convex, "cup", slope increasing)
     f'' < 0 on I  => f is CONCAVE DOWN ("cap", slope decreasing)
     Inflection point: a point where concavity changes (f'' changes
     sign); at such a point f'' = 0 or does not exist (necessary, not
     sufficient).
     SECOND-DERIVATIVE TEST: if f'(c) = 0 then
       f''(c) > 0 => local minimum at c
       f''(c) < 0 => local maximum at c
       f''(c) = 0 => test inconclusive (use the first-derivative test).
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: f'' is the rate of change of the slope (curvature,
   acceleration).
parts.D:
CONCEPT: concave up: the curve lies above its tangents and bends
   upward like a bowl: critical points there are minima. This
   reasoning generalizes to the Hessian in many variables (Module 12).
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: f'' must exist near c; the test is inconclusive when
   f''(c) = 0 (x^4 has a minimum, x^3 none, -x^4 a maximum).
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Using f(x) = x^3 - 3x + 1: f''(x) = 6x. f''(-1) = -6 < 0 (max);

F3.14  SECOND DERIVATIVE, CONCAVITY, SECOND-DERIVATIVE TEST
B. FORMULA/RULES
     f''(x) = d/dx [ f'(x) ]   (second derivative; also d^2 f/dx^2)

     f'' < 0 on I  => f is CONCAVE DOWN ("cap", slope decreasing)

     sign); at such a point f'' = 0 or does not exist (necessary, not
     sufficient).

       f''(c) < 0 => local maximum at c
       f''(c) = 0 => test inconclusive (use the first-derivative test).

   acceleration).

sections.title: INTERPRETING DERIVATIVE GRAPHS

blocks.rawText: Reading f from graphs of f' and f'' (a common exam skill):

Feature of the graph of f'           Meaning for f
  f' above the x-axis                  f increasing
  f' below the x-axis                  f decreasing
  f' crosses axis from + to -          local max of f
  f' crosses axis from - to +          local min of f
  f' touches axis, no sign change      no extremum (flat spot)
  f' increasing                        f concave up (f'' > 0)
  f' decreasing                        f concave down (f'' < 0)
  f' has a local max or min            f has an inflection point
  f' large in magnitude                f changing rapidly (steep)
  f' undefined (jump, spike)           corner or cusp of f

Reading f' from the graph of f: slope of the tangent at each point.
Reading f from f': area under f' gives change in f (Module 4).

WORKED EXAMPLE: f' is the line f'(x) = 2 - x on R. f' > 0 for x < 2 (f
increasing), f' < 0 for x > 2 (f decreasing); f' crosses + to - at 2
(local max); f' is decreasing everywhere so f'' = -1 < 0 (concave down).
One such f is f(x) = 2x - x^2/2 + C.

sections.title: PRACTICAL APPLICATIONS (CALCULUS TO DATA SCIENCE)

blocks.rawText:
1. Gradient descent: update w <- w - eta f'(w) moves downhill (Module
   43).
2. Maximum likelihood: set the derivative of the log-likelihood to 0
   (Module 38). Example below.
3. Sensitivity analysis: f'(x) dx approximates the effect of small
   changes.
4. Related rates & marginal analysis (economics: marginal cost = C'(x)).
5. Activation functions: sigmoid s' = s(1-s); tanh' = 1 - tanh^2;
   ReLU' = 0 or 1 (undefined at 0).

WORKED EXAMPLE (MLE preview, derivative = 0): n Bernoulli(p) trials give
k successes. Log-likelihood l(p) = k ln p + (n - k) ln(1 - p).
   l'(p) = k/p - (n - k)/(1 - p) = 0
   => k(1 - p) = (n - k) p => k = n p => p_hat = k/n.
   l''(p) = -k/p^2 - (n-k)/(1-p)^2 < 0, so it is a maximum. For n = 20,
   k = 7: p_hat = 0.35.

sections.title: ANTIDERIVATIVES AND INDEFINITE INTEGRALS

blocks.rawText:
BASIC IDEA (plain English)
Differentiation takes a function and gives its rate of change.
Integration runs the film backwards: given a rate of change, rebuild the
quantity. If a car's speed is known at every moment, integration gives
the distance traveled.

blocks.title: ANTIDERIVATIVE / INDEFINITE INTEGRAL
blocks.formulaBody:
F is an antiderivative of f if F'(x) = f(x).
     int f(x) dx = F(x) + C      (the family of ALL antiderivatives)

parts.B:
FORMULA
     F is an antiderivative of f if F'(x) = f(x).
     int f(x) dx = F(x) + C      (the family of ALL antiderivatives)
parts.C:
SYMBOLS
   int       the integral sign (an elongated S: "sum").
   f(x)      the integrand (function being integrated).
   dx        says "integrate with respect to x" (the variable).
   F(x)      any one antiderivative.
   C         arbitrary constant of integration; derivative of a constant
             is 0, so all antiderivatives of f differ by a constant.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: "Which functions have derivative f?" There are infinitely
   many, differing by constants: shifting a curve up/down does not change
   its slopes. C records this lost information; initial conditions
   (e.g. position at t = 0) pin it down.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: f continuous on the interval guarantees an antiderivative
   exists. An antiderivative can exist yet have NO formula in elementary
   functions (e.g. e^(-x^2); this is why the normal CDF is a named
   special function, Module 35).
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: int (3x^2 - 4x + 5) dx = x^3 - 2x^2 + 5x + C.
   Check by differentiating: 3x^2 - 4x + 5. OK.
   Moderate: A particle has velocity v(t) = 6t^2 - 4 and position
     s(0) = 3. s(t) = int v dt = 2t^3 - 4t + C; s(0) = C = 3, so
     s(t) = 2t^3 - 4t + 3.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: C is the "initial state". Always check an
   antiderivative by differentiating it.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: forgetting + C; applying the power rule with n = -1
   (int x^(-1) dx = ln|x| + C, not x^0/0).
parts.J:
RELATED: definite integral F4.2; differential equations (Module 15)
   are "find a function from its derivative" problems.

blocks.title: STANDARD INTEGRALS TABLE  (each is the derivative table reversed)
blocks.formulaBody:
int x^n dx   = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C            (n != -1)
     int 1/x dx   = ln|x| + C
     int e^x dx   = e^x + C
     int e^(kx) dx = e^(kx)/k + C                (k != 0)
     int a^x dx   = a^x/ln a + C                 (a > 0, a != 1)
     int sin x dx = -cos x + C
     int cos x dx = sin x + C
     int sec^2 x dx = tan x + C
     int 1/(1 + x^2) dx = arctan x + C
     int 1/sqrt(1 - x^2) dx = arcsin x + C
     int c f(x) dx = c int f dx;  int (f + g) dx = int f dx + int g dx.
   !! COMMON MISTAKE !! No product/quotient shortcut: int f g dx is NOT
   (int f dx)(int g dx).  Constants of integration from several terms
   are merged into one C.
   !! COMMON MISTAKE !! int 1/(x^2+1) dx is not ln(x^2+1).

blocks.title: DEFINITE INTEGRAL (RIEMANN SUM DEFINITION)
blocks.formulaBody:
int[a..b] f(x) dx = lim[n -> inf] sum[i=1..n] f(x_i*) * Dx
     where Dx = (b - a)/n  and x_i* is a sample point in the i-th
     subinterval.

parts.B:
FORMULA

sections.title: THE FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM OF CALCULUS (FTC)

blocks.title: FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM OF CALCULUS
blocks.formulaBody:
Part 1:  d/dx [ int[a..x] f(t) dt ] = f(x)
     Part 2:  int[a..b] f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a)      where F' = f
     Notation: F(b) - F(a) = [F(x)] evaluated from a to b.

parts.B:
FORMULAS
     Part 1:  d/dx [ int[a..x] f(t) dt ] = f(x)
     Part 2:  int[a..b] f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a)      where F' = f
     Notation: F(b) - F(a) = [F(x)] evaluated from a to b.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: t is a dummy variable (the integration variable inside);
   x is the upper limit (a variable); F is any antiderivative of f.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: Differentiation and integration are inverse operations.
   Part 1: the area function A(x) = int[a..x] f grows at rate f(x).
   Part 2: to compute an area, you only need an antiderivative at two
   endpoints: the total change in F equals the accumulated rate f.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: f continuous on [a, b]. In Part 2, the constant C cancels
   in F(b) - F(a), so no C is needed. If f has a discontinuity or an
   infinite spike inside [a,b], FTC must not be applied blindly
   (e.g. int[-1..1] 1/x^2 dx is NOT -2: the integrand blows up at 0).
g. the integral of marginal cost from 0 to 100 items is the total
   cost increase.
parts.F:
IDEA OF PROOF (Part 2): the change in F over [a,b] is the sum of
   tiny changes F(x_i) - F(x_(i-1)) which (by the mean value theorem)
   equal f(c_i) Dx; summing gives the Riemann sum for f, whose limit is
   the integral.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: int[0..2] (x^2 + 1) dx = [x^3/3 + x] from 0 to 2
           = 8/3 + 2 - 0 = 14/3 = 4.667.
   Moderate: int[0..pi] sin x dx = [-cos x] = -cos(pi) + cos(0)
           = 1 + 1 = 2.
   Moderate 2 (chain with Part 1): d/dx int[1..x^2] e^(t) dt
           = e^(x^2) * 2x  (Part 1 plus chain rule).
   Net vs total: int[0..2pi] sin x dx = 0 (positive and negative
           areas cancel), but total area = 2 * int[0..pi] sin x = 4.
parts.H: INTERPRETATION: net change theorem: int[a..b] f'(x) dx = f(b) - f(a).
parts.I:
MISTAKES: forgetting to evaluate at BOTH limits; subtracting in the
   wrong order; using FTC over a discontinuity.
parts.J:
RELATED: average value of f on [a,b] = (1/(b-a)) int[a..b] f dx;
   e.g. average of x^2 on [0,3] = (1/3)(9) = 3.

sections.title: SUBSTITUTION METHOD

blocks.title: u-SUBSTITUTION
blocks.formulaBody:
int f( g(x) ) g'(x) dx = int f(u) du,   with u = g(x), du = g'(x) dx.
   Definite form: int[a..b] f(g(x)) g'(x) dx = int[g(a)..g(b)] f(u) du.

parts.B:
FORMULA
     int f( g(x) ) g'(x) dx = int f(u) du,   with u = g(x), du = g'(x) dx.
   Definite form: int[a..b] f(g(x)) g'(x) dx = int[g(a)..g(b)] f(u) du.
parts.C: SYMBOLS: u the new variable; du = g'(x) dx its differential.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: It undoes the chain rule: spot an "inner function" whose
   derivative appears as a factor, and rename the inner function to
   simplify.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: g differentiable with continuous derivative; the
   integrand must contain g'(x) (up to a constant factor). In a
   definite integral, EITHER change the limits to u-values OR convert
   back to x before using the old limits; never mix them.
parts.F:
DERIVATION: from the chain rule d/dx F(g(x)) = F'(g(x)) g'(x) = f(g(x))
   g'(x) with F' = f.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: int 2x (x^2 + 1)^3 dx. u = x^2 + 1, du = 2x dx:
           int u^3 du = u^4/4 + C = (x^2 + 1)^4/4 + C.
   Moderate: int[0..1] x e^(x^2) dx. u = x^2, du = 2x dx, x dx = du/2.
           Limits: x=0 -> u=0; x=1 -> u=1.
           (1/2) int[0..1] e^u du = (1/2)(e - 1) = 0.8591.
   Moderate 2: int x/(x^2 + 4) dx = (1/2) ln(x^2 + 4) + C
           (u = x^2 + 4, du = 2x dx).
   Moderate 3: int cos(3x) dx = sin(3x)/3 + C.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: substitution is also the change of variables behind
   transformations of random variables and the Jacobian (Module 13).
parts.I:
MISTAKES: forgetting the constant factor (du = 2x dx but only x dx is
   present: introduce 1/2); not converting limits; leaving x in the
   integrand after substitution.
parts.J:
RELATED: the inverse of the chain rule (F3.7); change of variables
   with the Jacobian (F13.3); transformations of random variables
   (F36.5).

sections.title: INTEGRATION BY PARTS

blocks.title: INTEGRATION BY PARTS
blocks.formulaBody:
int u dv = u v - int v du
   i.e. int f(x) g'(x) dx = f(x) g(x) - int f'(x) g(x) dx.
   Definite: int[a..b] u dv = [u v] from a to b - int[a..b] v du.

parts.A: NAME: Integration by parts (reverse product rule).
parts.B:
FORMULA
     int u dv = u v - int v du
   i.e. int f(x) g'(x) dx = f(x) g(x) - int f'(x) g(x) dx.
   Definite: int[a..b] u dv = [u v] from a to b - int[a..b] v du.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: u = f(x) chosen to become SIMPLER when differentiated;
   dv = g'(x) dx chosen so v = int dv is EASY. du = f'(x) dx.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: Trades one integral for hopefully an easier one. Choose u by
   LIATE (priority): Logarithmic, Inverse trig, Algebraic (polynomial),
   Trigonometric, Exponential.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: f and g differentiable. Works best for a product of two
   different kinds of function. May need to be applied repeatedly or
   cyclically.
parts.F:
DERIVATION: product rule (uv)' = u'v + uv'. Integrate both sides:
   uv = int u'v dx + int u v' dx. Rearrange.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: int x e^x dx. u = x, dv = e^x dx -> du = dx, v = e^x.
           = x e^x - int e^x dx = x e^x - e^x + C = e^x (x - 1) + C.
           Check: d/dx [e^x (x-1)] = e^x (x-1) + e^x = x e^x. OK.
   Simple 2: int ln x dx. u = ln x, dv = dx -> du = dx/x, v = x.
           = x ln x - int 1 dx = x ln x - x + C.
           int[1..e] ln x dx = [x ln x - x] = (e - e) - (0 - 1) = 1.
   Moderate: int x^2 e^x dx. u = x^2, dv = e^x dx:
           = x^2 e^x - 2 int x e^x dx = x^2 e^x - 2 e^x (x - 1) + C
           = e^x (x^2 - 2x + 2) + C.
   Moderate 2 (expectation of the exponential distribution):
           E[X] = int[0..inf] x lambda e^(-lambda x) dx. u = x,
           dv = lambda e^(-lambda x) dx, v = -e^(-lambda x):
           = [-x e^(-lambda x)] from 0 to inf + int[0..inf] e^(-lambda x) dx
           = 0 + 1/lambda = 1/lambda.
           (The boundary term vanishes since x e^(-lambda x) -> 0, a
           growth-ranking fact from F2.4/2.3.)
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: integrals of the form x^n e^x and x^n ln x appear
   in moments of distributions and in the Gamma function.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: choosing u and dv the wrong way round (makes the integral
   harder); sign errors; forgetting the boundary term uv in definite
   integrals.
parts.J:
RELATED: tabular method for repeated parts; Gamma function
   Gamma(n) = int[0..inf] x^(n-1) e^(-x) dx = (n-1)! for integer n
   [SUPPLEMENTARY].

   Trigonometric, Exponential.
E. CONDITIONS: f and g differentiable. Works best for a product of two
   different kinds of function. May need to be applied repeatedly or
   cyclically.
F. DERIVATION: product rule (uv)' = u'v + uv'. Integrate both sides:
   uv = int u'v dx + int u v' dx. Rearrange.
G. EXAMPLES
   Simple: int x e^x dx. u = x, dv = e^x dx -> du = dx, v = e^x.
           = x e^x - int e^x dx = x e^x - e^x + C = e^x (x - 1) + C.
           Check: d/dx [e^x (x-1)] = e^x (x-1) + e^x = x e^x. OK.
   Simple 2: int ln x dx. u = ln x, dv = dx -> du = dx/x, v = x.
           = x ln x - int 1 dx = x ln x - x + C.
           int[1..e] ln x dx = [x ln x - x] = (e - e) - (0 - 1) = 1.
   Moderate: int x^2 e^x dx. u = x^2, dv = e^x dx:
           = x^2 e^x - 2 int x e^x dx = x^2 e^x - 2 e^x (x - 1) + C
           = e^x (x^2 - 2x + 2) + C.
   Moderate 2 (expectation of the exponential distribution):
           E[X] = int[0..inf] x lambda e^(-lambda x) dx. u = x,
           dv = lambda e^(-lambda x) dx, v = -e^(-lambda x):
           = [-x e^(-lambda x)] from 0 to inf + int[0..inf] e^(-lambda x) dx
           = 0 + 1/lambda = 1/lambda.

           growth-ranking fact from F2.4/2.3.)

   in moments of distributions and in the Gamma function.

   harder); sign errors; forgetting the boundary term uv in definite
   integrals.
J. RELATED: tabular method for repeated parts; Gamma function
   Gamma(n) = int[0..inf] x^(n-1) e^(-x) dx = (n-1)! for integer n
   [SUPPLEMENTARY].

blocks.rawText:
Covered in the table F4.2. Useful extra facts:
   int sin(kx) dx = -cos(kx)/k + C;  int cos(kx) dx = sin(kx)/k + C.

   Check: int[0..pi] sin^2 x dx = pi/2.
   Gaussian integral (no elementary antiderivative; stated, not derived):
     int[-inf..inf] e^(-x^2/2) dx = sqrt(2 pi).
   This is why the normal density has the constant 1/sqrt(2 pi).

sections.title: AREA UNDER A CURVE AND BETWEEN CURVES

blocks.title: AREA BETWEEN TWO CURVES
blocks.formulaBody:
Area = int[a..b] ( f(x) - g(x) ) dx   where f(x) >= g(x) on [a, b]
   (top minus bottom). If the curves cross, split at the intersections.
   Area under y = f(x) above the axis: int[a..b] f dx when f >= 0.

parts.B:
Area = int[a..b] ( f(x) - g(x) ) dx   where f(x) >= g(x) on [a, b]
   (top minus bottom). If the curves cross, split at the intersections.
   Area under y = f(x) above the axis: int[a..b] f dx when f >= 0.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: f upper curve; g lower curve; a, b the x-limits (often the
   intersection points).
parts.D: CONCEPT: stack thin vertical strips of height f - g and width dx.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: identify which curve is on top; take |...| / split when
   the order switches.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: area between y = x and y = x^2 on [0, 1]:
           int (x - x^2) dx = 1/2 - 1/3 = 1/6.
   Moderate: area enclosed by y = 2x and y = x^2:
           intersections: x^2 = 2x -> x = 0, 2. On (0,2): 2x >= x^2.
           int[0..2] (2x - x^2) dx = [x^2 - x^3/3] = 4 - 8/3 = 4/3.
   Moderate 2 (total area vs signed): area between y = x^2 - 4 and the
           x-axis over [-2, 2]: curve is below the axis (negative).
           int[-2..2] (x^2 - 4) dx = 2(8/3 - 8) = -32/3; area = 32/3.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: area between curves measures an accumulated
   difference; the area between an ROC curve and the diagonal equals AUC
   - 0.5.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: bottom minus top; ignoring crossings; using signed integral
   when asked for area.
parts.J:
RELATED: definite integral (F4.3); probabilities as areas under
   densities (F35.3).

sections.title: IMPROPER INTEGRALS AND CONVERGENCE

blocks.title: IMPROPER INTEGRAL
blocks.formulaBody:
int[a..inf] f(x) dx = lim[t -> inf] int[a..t] f(x) dx
     int[-inf..b] f(x) dx = lim[t -> -inf] int[t..b] f(x) dx
     int[-inf..inf] f dx = int[-inf..c] f + int[c..inf] f
        (BOTH must converge separately)
     If f is unbounded at x = a (a < b):
        int[a..b] f dx = lim[t -> a+] int[t..b] f dx.
   Converges if the limit is a finite number; otherwise diverges.

parts.A: NAME: Improper integral (infinite limit or unbounded integrand).
parts.B:
FORMULAS
     int[a..inf] f(x) dx = lim[t -> inf] int[a..t] f(x) dx
     int[-inf..b] f(x) dx = lim[t -> -inf] int[t..b] f(x) dx
     int[-inf..inf] f dx = int[-inf..c] f + int[c..inf] f
        (BOTH must converge separately)
     If f is unbounded at x = a (a < b):
        int[a..b] f dx = lim[t -> a+] int[t..b] f dx.
   Converges if the limit is a finite number; otherwise diverges.
parts.C: SYMBOLS: t the temporary finite endpoint, pushed to the problem point.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: an infinite region can still have finite area if the
   function decays quickly enough.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: break at interior singularities. Symmetric cancellation
   trick lim[t -> inf] int[-t..t] x dx = 0 does NOT make int[-inf..inf] x
   dx converge.
   P-TEST (standard benchmark):
     int[1..inf] 1/x^p dx converges iff p > 1, value 1/(p - 1).
     int[0..1]  1/x^p dx converges iff p < 1, value 1/(1 - p).
     int[0..inf] e^(-kx) dx = 1/k (k > 0).
   Comparison test: if 0 <= f <= g and int g converges then int f
   converges; if int f diverges then int g diverges.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: int[1..inf] 1/x^2 dx = lim (1 - 1/t) = 1.
           int[1..inf] 1/x dx = lim ln t = inf: DIVERGES.
   Moderate: int[0..1] 1/sqrt(x) dx = lim[t -> 0+] [2 sqrt(x)] from t to 1
           = 2 - 0 = 2 (converges).
   Moderate 2: int[0..inf] x e^(-x) dx = 1 (parts; = Gamma(2) = 1!).
   Moderate 3: int[-inf..inf] 1/(1 + x^2) dx = [arctan x] = pi/2 -
           (-pi/2) = pi. (Cauchy density: pi * (1/pi) = 1.)
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: a probability density must satisfy
   int[-inf..inf] f = 1, which is an improper integral that must
   converge. The mean of the Cauchy distribution does not exist
   because int x/(pi(1+x^2)) dx diverges.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: applying FTC across the singularity; treating
   inf - inf as zero; assuming all integrals to infinity diverge (or
   converge).
parts.J:
RELATED: series (Module 5): integral test links int[1..inf] f with
   sum f(n).

sections.title: SEQUENCES AND CONVERGENCE

blocks.rawText:
BASIC IDEA: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers a_1, a_2, a_3, ...
(a function from the positive integers). A sequence CONVERGES if its
terms settle toward one number as the position n grows.

blocks.title: CONVERGENCE OF A SEQUENCE
blocks.formulaBody:
lim[n -> inf] a_n = L   means: for every epsilon > 0 there is
   N such that n > N implies |a_n - L| < epsilon.

parts.B:
FORMULA: lim[n -> inf] a_n = L   means: for every epsilon > 0 there is
   N such that n > N implies |a_n - L| < epsilon.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: n position index (integer); a_n n-th term; L limit; N the
   point after which all terms are within epsilon of L.
parts.D: CONCEPT: same epsilon idea as F2.1, with integers.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: limit must be a finite number. Otherwise the sequence
   DIVERGES (to infinity or by oscillation). Limit laws (F2.2) apply.
   Monotone Convergence Theorem: every bounded monotone (always
   non-decreasing, or always non-increasing) sequence converges.
   If a_n = f(n) and lim[x -> inf] f(x) = L then a_n -> L.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Converges: a_n = n/(n + 1) -> 1 (divide by n: 1/(1 + 1/n)).
              a_n = (1 + 1/n)^n -> e. a_n = 1/2^n -> 0.
   Diverges:  a_n = (-1)^n oscillates between -1 and 1. a_n = n^2 -> inf.
   Recursive (Newton for sqrt(2)): a_(n+1) = (a_n + 2/a_n)/2, a_1 = 1:
              1, 1.5, 1.41667, 1.414216, ... -> sqrt(2) = 1.41421356.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: convergence means the sequence settles down
   (iterative algorithms, running averages); oscillation or growth means
   divergence.
parts.J:
RELATED: limits of functions (F2.1), series (F5.3), consistency of
   estimators (F37.7).

blocks.rawText:
F5.1  CONVERGENCE OF A SEQUENCE
A. NAME: Limit of a sequence.
B. FORMULA: lim[n -> inf] a_n = L   means: for every epsilon > 0 there is
   N such that n > N implies |a_n - L| < epsilon.
C. SYMBOLS: n position index (integer); a_n n-th term; L limit; N the
   point after which all terms are within epsilon of L.
D. CONCEPT: same epsilon idea as F2.1, with integers.
E. CONDITIONS: limit must be a finite number. Otherwise the sequence
   DIVERGES (to infinity or by oscillation). Limit laws (F2.2) apply.
   Monotone Convergence Theorem: every bounded monotone (always
   non-decreasing, or always non-increasing) sequence converges.
   If a_n = f(n) and lim[x -> inf] f(x) = L then a_n -> L.
G. EXAMPLES
   Converges: a_n = n/(n + 1) -> 1 (divide by n: 1/(1 + 1/n)).
              a_n = (1 + 1/n)^n -> e. a_n = 1/2^n -> 0.
   Diverges:  a_n = (-1)^n oscillates between -1 and 1. a_n = n^2 -> inf.
   Recursive (Newton for sqrt(2)): a_(n+1) = (a_n + 2/a_n)/2, a_1 = 1:
              1, 1.5, 1.41667, 1.414216, ... -> sqrt(2) = 1.41421356.
H. INTERPRETATION: convergence means the sequence settles down
   (iterative algorithms, running averages); oscillation or growth means
   divergence.
I. MISTAKE: "the terms get closer to each other, so it converges" is true
   for sequences (Cauchy) but the analogous idea for series is wrong:
   terms -> 0 does not make a series converge.
J. RELATED: limits of functions (F2.1), series (F5.3), consistency of
   estimators (F37.7).

blocks.title: ARITHMETIC AND GEOMETRIC SEQUENCES
blocks.formulaBody:

sections.rawText:
BASIC IDEA: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers a_1, a_2, a_3, ...
(a function from the positive integers). A sequence CONVERGES if its
terms settle toward one number as the position n grows.

F5.1  CONVERGENCE OF A SEQUENCE
A. NAME: Limit of a sequence.
B. FORMULA: lim[n -> inf] a_n = L   means: for every epsilon > 0 there is
   N such that n > N implies |a_n - L| < epsilon.
C. SYMBOLS: n position index (integer); a_n n-th term; L limit; N the
   point after which all terms are within epsilon of L.
D. CONCEPT: same epsilon idea as F2.1, with integers.
E. CONDITIONS: limit must be a finite number. Otherwise the sequence
   DIVERGES (to infinity or by oscillation). Limit laws (F2.2) apply.
   Monotone Convergence Theorem: every bounded monotone (always
   non-decreasing, or always non-increasing) sequence converges.
   If a_n = f(n) and lim[x -> inf] f(x) = L then a_n -> L.
G. EXAMPLES
   Converges: a_n = n/(n + 1) -> 1 (divide by n: 1/(1 + 1/n)).
              a_n = (1 + 1/n)^n -> e. a_n = 1/2^n -> 0.
   Diverges:  a_n = (-1)^n oscillates between -1 and 1. a_n = n^2 -> inf.
   Recursive (Newton for sqrt(2)): a_(n+1) = (a_n + 2/a_n)/2, a_1 = 1:
              1, 1.5, 1.41667, 1.414216, ... -> sqrt(2) = 1.41421356.
H. INTERPRETATION: convergence means the sequence settles down
   (iterative algorithms, running averages); oscillation or growth means
   divergence.
I. MISTAKE: "the terms get closer to each other, so it converges" is true
   for sequences (Cauchy) but the analogous idea for series is wrong:
   terms -> 0 does not make a series converge.
J. RELATED: limits of functions (F2.1), series (F5.3), consistency of
   estimators (F37.7).

blocks.title: INFINITE SERIES, PARTIAL SUMS AND THE GEOMETRIC SERIES
blocks.formulaBody:
Series:  sum[k=1..inf] a_k = lim[n -> inf] S_n, S_n = a_1+...+a_n
              (S_n are the PARTIAL SUMS). Converges iff S_n converges.
     Geometric series:  sum[k=0..inf] a r^k = a / (1 - r),   |r| < 1.
                        Diverges if |r| >= 1 (and a != 0).

parts.B:
FORMULAS
     Series:  sum[k=1..inf] a_k = lim[n -> inf] S_n, S_n = a_1+...+a_n
              (S_n are the PARTIAL SUMS). Converges iff S_n converges.
     Geometric series:  sum[k=0..inf] a r^k = a / (1 - r),   |r| < 1.
                        Diverges if |r| >= 1 (and a != 0).
parts.C: SYMBOLS: a first term; r common ratio; S_n n-th partial sum.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: adding infinitely many numbers can give a finite total if
   the terms shrink fast enough. Geometric: each term is a fixed fraction
   of the last (1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + ... = 2: keep halving the remaining
   distance to a wall).
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: the geometric series converges only for |r| < 1; the
   formula a/(1 - r) uses the FIRST term a, so the start index matters.
parts.F:
DERIVATION: S_n = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r) (F5.2). If |r| < 1, r^n -> 0, so
   S_n -> a/(1 - r).
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: sum[k=0..inf] (1/2)^k = 1/(1 - 1/2) = 2.
   Moderate 1: sum[k=1..inf] 3 (2/5)^k: first term a = 6/5, r = 2/5;
        sum = (6/5)/(1 - 2/5) = (6/5)/(3/5) = 2.
   Moderate 2 (repeating decimal): 0.272727... = 0.27 + 0.0027 + ...
        a = 0.27, r = 0.01: sum = 0.27/0.99 = 27/99 = 3/11.
   Applied: expected discounted reward in RL with reward 1 each step and
        discount gamma = 0.9: sum[k=0..inf] 0.9^k = 10.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: the sum is the limiting total of a repeating process
   (for instance total discounted reward).
parts.I:
MISTAKES: using the formula when |r| >= 1; using the wrong first term
   when the sum starts at k = 1 instead of 0 (the first term is a r, not
   a).
parts.J: RELATED: power series (5.4) generalize it: 1/(1-x) = sum x^k.

blocks.title: CONVERGENCE TESTS (a toolbox)
blocks.formulaBody:
Let sum a_k be a series.
 1. nth-TERM (DIVERGENCE) TEST: if lim a_k != 0 (or does not exist),
    the series DIVERGES. If lim a_k = 0 the test says NOTHING.
    !! WARNING !! Harmonic series sum 1/k has terms -> 0 but DIVERGES
    (partial sums grow like ln n).
 2. P-SERIES: sum[k=1..inf] 1/k^p converges iff p > 1.
    (p = 1 harmonic diverges; p = 2 converges to pi^2/6 [stated].)
 3. GEOMETRIC: converges iff |r| < 1.
 4. COMPARISON TEST: if 0 <= a_k <= b_k and sum b_k converges then
    sum a_k converges; if sum a_k diverges, sum b_k diverges.
 5. LIMIT COMPARISON: if a_k, b_k > 0 and lim a_k / b_k = c with
    0 < c < inf, both series converge or both diverge.
 6. INTEGRAL TEST: if a_k = f(k) with f positive, continuous, decreasing,
    then sum a_k and int[1..inf] f dx converge or diverge together.
 7. RATIO TEST: let rho = lim |a_(k+1) / a_k|.
       rho < 1 -> converges absolutely; rho > 1 -> diverges;
       rho = 1 -> inconclusive.
 8. ROOT TEST: rho = lim |a_k|^(1/k); same conclusions.
 9. ALTERNATING SERIES TEST (Leibniz): for sum (-1)^k b_k with b_k > 0,
    decreasing, and b_k -> 0, the series converges. The error after n
    terms is at most the first omitted term b_(n+1).
 10. TELESCOPING: terms cancel pairwise, e.g.
     sum[k=1..inf] 1/(k(k+1)) = sum (1/k - 1/(k+1)) = 1 (S_n = 1 - 1/(n+1)).

WORKED EXAMPLES
   Ratio test: sum k!/ (3^k)?  a_(k+1)/a_k = (k+1)/3 -> inf: DIVERGES.
   Ratio test: sum 2^k / k!: ratio = 2/(k+1) -> 0 < 1: converges.

ratio test and concluding convergence when rho = 1; using the integral
test when f is not decreasing; applying the comparison test in the wrong
direction (a smaller divergent series says nothing about a bigger one...
if a_k <= b_k and sum b_k diverges, nothing follows).

ratio test and concluding convergence when rho = 1; using the integral
test when f is not decreasing; applying the comparison test in the wrong
direction (a smaller divergent series says nothing about a bigger one...
if a_k <= b_k and sum b_k diverges, nothing follows).

sections.title: ABSOLUTE AND CONDITIONAL CONVERGENCE

blocks.rawText:
DEFINITIONS
   sum a_k converges ABSOLUTELY if sum |a_k| converges.
   It converges CONDITIONALLY if sum a_k converges but sum |a_k| diverges.
   THEOREM: absolute convergence implies convergence.
   Absolutely convergent series can be rearranged freely without changing
   the sum; for conditionally convergent series, Riemann's rearrangement
   theorem says rearrangements can give ANY value.
   EXAMPLES: sum (-1)^(k+1)/k^2: absolutely convergent (|terms| = 1/k^2).
             sum (-1)^(k+1)/k : conditionally convergent.
D. INTERPRETATION: absolute convergence is the robust, "safe" kind:
   needed to swap sums and integrals in expectation calculations.

sections.title: POWER SERIES, RADIUS AND INTERVAL OF CONVERGENCE

blocks.title: POWER SERIES
blocks.formulaBody:
f(x) = sum[n=0..inf] c_n (x - a)^n
     Radius of convergence R (ratio form):  R = lim[n -> inf] |c_n / c_(n+1)|
                         (if the limit exists)  or  1/R = lim |c_n|^(1/n).
     Converges absolutely for |x - a| < R; diverges for |x - a| > R;
     endpoints x = a +/- R must be tested separately.

sections.title: TAYLOR AND MACLAURIN SERIES

blocks.title: TAYLOR SERIES
blocks.formulaBody:
f(x) = sum[n=0..inf] ( f^(n)(a) / n! ) (x - a)^n
          = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + f''(a)/2 (x-a)^2 + f'''(a)/6 (x-a)^3 + ...
   Taylor polynomial of degree N: T_N(x) = sum[n=0..N] f^(n)(a)/n! (x-a)^n.
   Remainder (Lagrange form): f(x) - T_N(x) = f^(N+1)(xi)/(N+1)! (x-a)^(N+1)
   for some xi between a and x.

parts.A: NAME: Taylor series (Maclaurin series when a = 0).
parts.B:
FORMULA
     f(x) = sum[n=0..inf] ( f^(n)(a) / n! ) (x - a)^n
          = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + f''(a)/2 (x-a)^2 + f'''(a)/6 (x-a)^3 + ...
   Taylor polynomial of degree N: T_N(x) = sum[n=0..N] f^(n)(a)/n! (x-a)^n.
   Remainder (Lagrange form): f(x) - T_N(x) = f^(N+1)(xi)/(N+1)! (x-a)^(N+1)
   for some xi between a and x.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: f^(n)(a) = n-th derivative of f at a (f^(0) = f);
   n! factorial; xi ("xi") an unknown point between a and x.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: match f at a in value, slope, curvature, and so on. Each
   additional derivative adds a correction term, making the polynomial
   hug f ever more tightly. Degree 1 = tangent line (F3.2); degree 2 adds
   curvature (used in Newton's method and the Hessian approximation).
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: f infinitely differentiable at a; the series equals f only
   where the remainder -> 0 (inside the interval of convergence, for
   "analytic" functions). Not every infinitely differentiable function
   equals its Taylor series [Level 3: e^(-1/x^2)].
parts.F:
DERIVATION IDEA: assume f = sum c_n (x-a)^n, differentiate n times,
   set x = a: f^(n)(a) = n! c_n.
parts.G:
KEY MACLAURIN SERIES (center 0)
     e^x     = sum x^n/n!                       = 1 + x + x^2/2! + x^3/3! + ...   (all x)
     sin x   = sum (-1)^k x^(2k+1)/(2k+1)!       = x - x^3/3! + x^5/5! - ...       (all x)
     cos x   = sum (-1)^k x^(2k)/(2k)!           = 1 - x^2/2! + x^4/4! - ...       (all x)
     1/(1-x) = sum x^n                           = 1 + x + x^2 + ...               (|x| < 1)
     ln(1+x) = sum (-1)^(n+1) x^n / n            = x - x^2/2 + x^3/3 - ...         (-1 < x <= 1)
     (1+x)^alpha = sum C(alpha, n) x^n    (|x| < 1)
                 = 1 + alpha x + alpha(alpha-1)/2 x^2 + ...
     arctan x = sum (-1)^n x^(2n+1)/(2n+1)       = x - x^3/3 + x^5/5 - ...         (|x| <= 1)
   EXAMPLES
   Simple: e^1 approx 1 + 1 + 1/2 + 1/6 + 1/24 = 2.70833 (degree 4);
        true e = 2.71828; Lagrange bound on error:
        e^xi/5! <= e/120 = 0.0227 (actual error 0.00995, within bound).
   Moderate 1: sin(0.5) approx 0.5 - 0.5^3/6 = 0.5 - 0.0208333 = 0.479167
        (true 0.479426). Next term +0.5^5/120 = 0.00026 -> 0.479427.
   Moderate 2: derive the Maclaurin series of f(x) = ln(1 + x):
        f(0) = 0; f' = 1/(1+x) -> 1; f'' = -1/(1+x)^2 -> -1;
        f''' = 2/(1+x)^3 -> 2; f'''' = -6/(1+x)^4 -> -6.
        Coefficients: 0, 1, -1/2!, 2/3!, -6/4! = x - x^2/2 + x^3/3 - x^4/4.
   Moderate 3 (second-order approximation): sqrt(1 + x) approx
        1 + x/2 - x^2/8 for small x. x = 0.1: 1 + 0.05 - 0.00125
        = 1.04875; true 1.0488088.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: Taylor polynomials give LOCAL approximations: errors
   grow away from the center. Data science: second-order expansion of a
   loss around the current parameters = Newton's method (Module 43);
   first-order = gradient descent; log-odds approximations for small
   probabilities.
parts.J:
RELATED: tangent-line approximation (F3.2); binomial theorem F1.7
   (finite case of the binomial series).

sections.title: TERM-BY-TERM DIFFERENTIATION AND INTEGRATION; GEOMETRIC-SERIES REPRESENTATIONS OF FUNCTIONS

blocks.title: TERM-BY-TERM CALCULUS
blocks.formulaBody:
If f(x) = sum c_n (x - a)^n has radius R > 0, then for |x - a| < R:
     f'(x) = sum n c_n (x - a)^(n-1)
     int f(x) dx = C + sum c_n (x - a)^(n+1)/(n + 1)
   Both new series have the SAME radius R (but endpoint behavior may
   change).

parts.B:
If f(x) = sum c_n (x - a)^n has radius R > 0, then for |x - a| < R:
     f'(x) = sum n c_n (x - a)^(n-1)
     int f(x) dx = C + sum c_n (x - a)^(n+1)/(n + 1)
   Both new series have the SAME radius R (but endpoint behavior may
   change).
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: c_n coefficients; a the center; R the radius of convergence;
   f' and int f the new series.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: a power series behaves like a polynomial inside its interval
   of convergence.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: valid only inside |x - a| < R; at the endpoints
   convergence must be rechecked.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES (from the geometric series 1/(1-x) = sum x^n, |x| < 1)
   Differentiate: 1/(1-x)^2 = sum n x^(n-1) = 1 + 2x + 3x^2 + ...
   Integrate:  -ln(1 - x) = sum x^(n+1)/(n+1) = x + x^2/2 + x^3/3 + ...
   Replace x by -x^2: 1/(1+x^2) = sum (-1)^n x^(2n), |x| < 1. Integrate:
        arctan x = sum (-1)^n x^(2n+1)/(2n+1).
   Replace x by x/2 and multiply by 1/2: 1/(2 - x) = (1/2) sum (x/2)^n,
        |x| < 2.
   Expected value of the geometric distribution (Module 35): with
        q = 1 - p, sum[k=1..inf] k q^(k-1) p = p * 1/(1-q)^2 = 1/p.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: gives series for new functions (1/(1 - x)^2, -ln(1 -
   x), arctan x) from known ones.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: differentiating at the boundary of the interval; claiming
   the interval of convergence stays the same (endpoints can change).

    valid for |x| < 4.

   of the geometric distribution (Module 35).

approximations; series convergence matters for the correctness of
iterative algorithms.

F5.7  TERM-BY-TERM CALCULUS
B. If f(x) = sum c_n (x - a)^n has radius R > 0, then for |x - a| < R:
     f'(x) = sum n c_n (x - a)^(n-1)
     int f(x) dx = C + sum c_n (x - a)^(n+1)/(n + 1)
   Both new series have the SAME radius R (but endpoint behavior may
   change).
C. SYMBOLS: c_n coefficients; a the center; R the radius of convergence;
   f' and int f the new series.
D. CONCEPT: a power series behaves like a polynomial inside its interval
   of convergence.
E. CONDITIONS: valid only inside |x - a| < R; at the endpoints
   convergence must be rechecked.
G. EXAMPLES (from the geometric series 1/(1-x) = sum x^n, |x| < 1)
   Differentiate: 1/(1-x)^2 = sum n x^(n-1) = 1 + 2x + 3x^2 + ...
   Integrate:  -ln(1 - x) = sum x^(n+1)/(n+1) = x + x^2/2 + x^3/3 + ...
   Replace x by -x^2: 1/(1+x^2) = sum (-1)^n x^(2n), |x| < 1. Integrate:

   x), arctan x) from known ones.

sections.title: SCALARS, VECTORS AND MATRICES

blocks.rawText:
BASIC IDEA (plain English)
  scalar : a single number (3, -0.5, pi).
  vector : an ordered list of numbers; can be a point or an arrow in
           space, or simply a data record (age, height, income).
  matrix : a rectangular grid of numbers; can be a table of data, or a
           machine that transforms vectors (rotate, stretch, project).

NOTATION
  Scalar:  a, b, lambda (lower case italic).
  Vector:  v = (v1, v2, ..., vn)^T  : a column of n entries (an element
           of R^n). Entries are v_i (subscript i = position).
  Matrix:  A with m rows and n columns is "m x n" ("m by n"); entry in
           row i, column j is a_ij (or A[i][j]); A is in R^(m x n).
           Written row by row: A = [a11 a12 ; a21 a22].
  A vector is an n x 1 matrix (column vector); the transpose v^T is a
  1 x n row vector.

blocks.title: COMPARISON TABLE: SCALAR vs VECTOR vs MATRIX
blocks.rawText:
Object   Shape      Example               Typical meaning
  Scalar   1 x 1      5                     magnitude, weight, learning rate
  Vector   n x 1      (2, -1, 4)^T          point, direction, feature row
  Matrix   m x n      [1 2 ; 3 4]           dataset (rows = samples), linear
                                            map, covariance table
  (Tensor  higher-dim arrays: images (H x W x 3), batches [SUPPLEMENTARY])
  Order of data-science convention: a dataset X has n rows (samples) and
  p columns (features): X is n x p. A single sample x_i is a p-vector.

F6.1  VECTOR ADDITION AND SCALAR MULTIPLICATION
B. u + v = (u1 + v1, ..., un + vn);   c v = (c v1, ..., c vn).

blocks.title: DOT (INNER) PRODUCT
blocks.formulaBody: u . v = u^T v = sum[i=1..n] u_i v_i = |u| |v| cos(theta)

parts.A: NAME: Dot product (standard inner product on R^n).
parts.B:
FORMULA
     u . v = u^T v = sum[i=1..n] u_i v_i = |u| |v| cos(theta)
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: u_i, v_i entries; |u| the length (norm) of u;
   theta the angle between u and v (0 <= theta <= pi).
parts.D:
CONCEPT: measures how much two vectors point the same way. Positive:
   angle < 90 degrees; zero: perpendicular (orthogonal); negative:
   angle > 90 degrees. The result is a SCALAR.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: same length. Symmetric: u.v = v.u; bilinear;
   u.u = |u|^2 >= 0, and = 0 only for the zero vector.
parts.F:
DERIVATION of the cosine form: the law of cosines applied to the
   triangle with sides u, v, u - v:
   |u - v|^2 = |u|^2 + |v|^2 - 2|u||v|cos(theta). Expanding the left
   side via dot products, |u - v|^2 = |u|^2 - 2 u.v + |v|^2, so
   u.v = |u||v|cos(theta).
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: (1,2,3).(4,-5,6) = 4 - 10 + 18 = 12.
   Moderate: angle between a = (1, 0) and b = (1, 1):
        a.b = 1; |a| = 1; |b| = sqrt(2); cos(theta) = 1/sqrt(2) ->
        theta = 45 degrees (pi/4).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: cosine similarity cos(theta) = u.v/(|u||v|) compares
   documents/embeddings by direction regardless of length. A linear
   model prediction is a dot product w.x + b.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: confusing the dot product (scalar) with the cross product
   (vector, 3D only) or with element-wise multiplication (a vector;
   Python u * v on NumPy arrays is element-wise!). Using it on vectors
   of different lengths.
parts.J: RELATED: norm (F6.3), orthogonality and projection (Module 10).

blocks.title: NORM (LENGTH) OF A VECTOR
blocks.formulaBody:
Euclidean (L2) norm |v|_2 = sqrt(v1^2 + ... + vn^2)
            = sqrt(v . v).
   Other norms: L1: |v|_1 = |v1| + ... + |vn|;
                L-infinity: |v|_inf = max_i |v_i|.
   Unit vector in the direction of v: v / |v| (v != 0).

parts.B:
FORMULA: Euclidean (L2) norm |v|_2 = sqrt(v1^2 + ... + vn^2)
            = sqrt(v . v).
   Other norms: L1: |v|_1 = |v1| + ... + |vn|;
                L-infinity: |v|_inf = max_i |v_i|.
   Unit vector in the direction of v: v / |v| (v != 0).
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: v_i the components; |v|_1, |v|_2, |v|_inf the L1, L2 and
   maximum norms.
parts.D: CONCEPT: Pythagoras in n dimensions. L1 is "city-block" distance.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: v != 0 for a unit vector; every norm satisfies |v| >= 0
   (= 0 only for the zero vector), |c v| = |c||v|, and the triangle
   inequality.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES: v = (3, 4): |v|_2 = 5, |v|_1 = 7, |v|_inf = 4. Unit vector
   (0.6, 0.8). Distance between points p and q = |p - q|_2.
   u = (1,2,3): |u| = sqrt(14) = 3.742.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: the norm is the size of the vector (distance from the
   origin); |p - q|_2 is Euclidean distance (F11.1).
parts.I:
MISTAKE: forgetting the square root; mixing L1/L2 in regularization
   (Lasso = L1, Ridge = L2).
parts.J: RELATED: Euclidean distance; regularization penalties; MAE vs RMSE.

blocks.title: CROSS PRODUCT [SUPPLEMENTARY; R^3 ONLY]
blocks.formulaBody:
u x v = (u2 v3 - u3 v2, u3 v1 - u1 v3, u1 v2 - u2 v1). Result is
   perpendicular to both; |u x v| = |u||v| sin(theta) = area of the
   parallelogram spanned. Used for normals to planes (Module 11).

parts.B:
u x v = (u2 v3 - u3 v2, u3 v1 - u1 v3, u1 v2 - u2 v1). Result is
   perpendicular to both; |u x v| = |u||v| sin(theta) = area of the
   parallelogram spanned. Used for normals to planes (Module 11).
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: u = (u1, u2, u3), v = (v1, v2, v3); x the cross-product
   symbol; theta the angle between the vectors.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the cross product is perpendicular to both inputs
   (right-hand rule), with length equal to the area of the parallelogram
   they span.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: defined only in R^3; anti-commutative (u x v = -(v x u));
   u x v = 0 exactly when u and v are parallel.
parts.G: (1,0,0) x (0,1,0) = (0,0,1).  Anti-commutative: v x u = -(u x v).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: gives normal vectors of planes (F11.4), areas and
   torques.
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: confusing it with the dot product (a vector versus a
   scalar); applying it in dimensions other than 3.
parts.J:
RELATED: dot product (F6.2), plane equation (F11.4), determinant as
   area (F6.9).

blocks.title: TRANSPOSE
blocks.formulaBody:
(A^T)_ij = a_ji (rows become columns).
   Rules: (A^T)^T = A;  (A + B)^T = A^T + B^T;  (cA)^T = c A^T;
          (AB)^T = B^T A^T.
   Symmetric matrix: A^T = A (requires square). Skew-symmetric: A^T = -A.

parts.B:

sections.title: INVERSE MATRICES

blocks.title: MATRIX INVERSE
blocks.formulaBody:
A^(-1) is the matrix with A A^(-1) = A^(-1) A = I.
   2x2 closed form: for A = [a b ; c d] with det(A) = ad - bc != 0,
        A^(-1) = (1/(ad - bc)) [ d  -b ; -c  a ].
   Properties: (A^(-1))^(-1) = A; (AB)^(-1) = B^(-1) A^(-1);
               (A^T)^(-1) = (A^(-1))^T; (cA)^(-1) = (1/c) A^(-1).

parts.A: NAME: Inverse of a square matrix.
parts.B:
FORMULA: A^(-1) is the matrix with A A^(-1) = A^(-1) A = I.
   2x2 closed form: for A = [a b ; c d] with det(A) = ad - bc != 0,
        A^(-1) = (1/(ad - bc)) [ d  -b ; -c  a ].
   Properties: (A^(-1))^(-1) = A; (AB)^(-1) = B^(-1) A^(-1);
               (A^T)^(-1) = (A^(-1))^T; (cA)^(-1) = (1/c) A^(-1).
parts.C: SYMBOLS: I identity; a, b, c, d the four entries.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: A^(-1) undoes A. If A stretches/rotates the plane, A^(-1)
   puts it back. Exists only if A loses no information (does not
   squash space onto a lower dimension).
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: A must be SQUARE and non-singular (det != 0, equivalently
   rank n, linearly independent columns, Ax = 0 has only x = 0). A
   non-square matrix has no (two-sided) inverse.
   !! WARNING !! For numerical work, NEVER compute A^(-1) just to solve
   Ax = b; use elimination (np.linalg.solve). Inverting is slower and
   less accurate.
parts.F:
DERIVATION (2x2): solve A X = I column by column, or verify:
   [a b ; c d][d -b ; -c a] = [ad - bc, 0 ; 0, ad - bc] = (ad-bc) I.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: the inverse exists iff the transformation is
   reversible. Near-singular matrices (tiny determinant relative to
   the entries, huge condition number) give unstable results.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: inverting a non-square or singular matrix; (AB)^(-1) =
   A^(-1) B^(-1) (WRONG order); thinking A^(-1) means 1/A element-wise.
parts.J:
RELATED: pseudo-inverse for non-square / rank-deficient matrices
   (Module 10); normal equations beta = (X^T X)^(-1) X^T y (Module 40).

G. EXAMPLES
   Simple: A = [4 7 ; 2 6]. det = 24 - 14 = 10.
        A^(-1) = (1/10)[6 -7 ; -2 4] = [0.6 -0.7 ; -0.2 0.4].
        Check row 1 of A times columns of A^(-1): 4*0.6 + 7*(-0.2) = 1;
        4*(-0.7) + 7*0.4 = 0. OK. Row 2: 2*0.6 + 6*(-0.2) = 0;
        2*(-0.7) + 6*0.4 = 1. OK.
   Moderate: Solve Ax = b with A above and b = (1, 2)^T using the inverse:
        x = A^(-1) b = (0.6*1 - 0.7*2, -0.2*1 + 0.4*2)^T = (-0.8, 0.6)^T.
        Check: 4*(-0.8) + 7*0.6 = -3.2 + 4.2 = 1; 2*(-0.8) + 6*0.6
        = -1.6 + 3.6 = 2. OK.
   Singular example: [1 2 ; 2 4] has det 0 (row 2 = 2 x row 1): no
        inverse.
   3x3 known pair: A = [1 2 3 ; 0 1 4 ; 5 6 0] has det 1 and
        A^(-1) = [-24 18 5 ; 20 -15 -4 ; -5 4 1].

sections.title: DETERMINANTS

blocks.title: DETERMINANT
blocks.formulaBody:
2x2:  det [a b ; c d] = ad - bc.
     3x3 (cofactor expansion along row 1):
       det A = a11 (a22 a33 - a23 a32) - a12 (a21 a33 - a23 a31)
             + a13 (a21 a32 - a22 a31).
     General (Laplace expansion along row i):
       det A = sum[j=1..n] (-1)^(i+j) a_ij M_ij,
       where M_ij = determinant of A with row i and column j deleted.
     Triangular or diagonal matrix: det = product of the diagonal entries.

parts.A: NAME: Determinant of a square matrix.
parts.B:
FORMULAS
     2x2:  det [a b ; c d] = ad - bc.
     3x3 (cofactor expansion along row 1):
       det A = a11 (a22 a33 - a23 a32) - a12 (a21 a33 - a23 a31)
             + a13 (a21 a32 - a22 a31).
     General (Laplace expansion along row i):
       det A = sum[j=1..n] (-1)^(i+j) a_ij M_ij,
       where M_ij = determinant of A with row i and column j deleted.
     Triangular or diagonal matrix: det = product of the diagonal entries.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: a_ij entries; M_ij the (i,j) MINOR; (-1)^(i+j) the checkerboard
   sign pattern + - + / - + - / + - + ...
parts.D:
CONCEPT: det(A) is the SIGNED FACTOR by which the linear map x -> Ax
   scales areas (2D) or volumes (3D). det = 0: the map flattens space
   onto a lower dimension (loses information; singular). Negative:
   orientation flipped (a reflection).

A. NAME: Determinant of a square matrix.
B. FORMULAS
     2x2:  det [a b ; c d] = ad - bc.

             + a13 (a21 a32 - a22 a31).
     General (Laplace expansion along row i):
       det A = sum[j=1..n] (-1)^(i+j) a_ij M_ij,
       where M_ij = determinant of A with row i and column j deleted.
     Triangular or diagonal matrix: det = product of the diagonal entries.
C. SYMBOLS: a_ij entries; M_ij the (i,j) MINOR; (-1)^(i+j) the checkerboard
   sign pattern + - + / - + - / + - + ...
D. CONCEPT: det(A) is the SIGNED FACTOR by which the linear map x -> Ax
   scales areas (2D) or volumes (3D). det = 0: the map flattens space
   onto a lower dimension (loses information; singular). Negative:
   orientation flipped (a reflection).

     det(AB) = det(A) det(B);  det(A^T) = det(A);

sections.title: MATRIX REPRESENTATION OF LINEAR SYSTEMS

blocks.rawText:
A system of m linear equations in n unknowns
     a11 x1 + a12 x2 + ... + a1n xn = b1
     ...
     am1 x1 + am2 x2 + ... + amn xn = bm
is written compactly as    A x = b,
     A (m x n): COEFFICIENT matrix;  x (n x 1): vector of unknowns;
     b (m x 1): right-hand side.
Augmented matrix [A | b] stores everything needed for elimination.
Column view: Ax = x1 (column 1 of A) + ... + xn (column n of A): the
system asks "can b be built as a linear combination of A's columns?"
Row view: each equation is a hyperplane (line in 2D, plane in 3D); a
solution is a point lying on all of them.
Example: 2x + y = 5, x - y = 1 -> A = [2 1 ; 1 -1], x = (x, y)^T,
b = (5, 1)^T. Solution (2, 1): 4 + 1 = 5 and 2 - 1 = 1.

blocks.text:
regression normal equations (X^T X) beta = X^T y are
a linear system; PageRank, Markov chains and Gaussian process
predictions all solve linear systems.

sections.title: LINEAR EQUATIONS IN SEVERAL VARIABLES

blocks.rawText:
LINEAR EQUATION: a1 x1 + ... + an xn = b with constant coefficients: no
products or powers of unknowns, no functions of unknowns (x1 x2,
x^2, sin x are non-linear).
GEOMETRY OF 2 EQUATIONS IN 2 UNKNOWNS: two lines.
   intersect at one point     -> unique solution
   parallel and distinct      -> no solution (inconsistent)
   the same line              -> infinitely many solutions
3 equations in 3 unknowns: three planes (single point, a line,
a plane, or none).

sections.title: GAUSSIAN ELIMINATION, ROW ECHELON AND REDUCED ROW ECHELON FORM

blocks.title: ELEMENTARY ROW OPERATIONS AND GAUSSIAN ELIMINATION
blocks.formulaBody:
THE THREE ELEMENTARY ROW OPERATIONS (do not change the solution set)
     (1) Swap two rows:                R_i <-> R_j
     (2) Multiply a row by a nonzero scalar:   R_i <- c R_i  (c != 0)
     (3) Add a multiple of one row to another: R_i <- R_i + c R_j

parts.B:
THE THREE ELEMENTARY ROW OPERATIONS (do not change the solution set)
     (1) Swap two rows:                R_i <-> R_j
     (2) Multiply a row by a nonzero scalar:   R_i <- c R_i  (c != 0)
     (3) Add a multiple of one row to another: R_i <- R_i + c R_j
parts.C: SYMBOLS: R_i = row i of the augmented matrix.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: systematically eliminate unknowns, creating a triangular
   ("staircase") system that can be solved from the bottom up (back
   substitution). Each operation corresponds to multiplying on the left
   by an invertible matrix, hence does not change the solutions.
parts.E:
DEFINITIONS
   ROW ECHELON FORM (REF):
     - any all-zero rows are at the bottom;
     - the leading entry (first nonzero entry, the PIVOT) of each nonzero
       row lies to the right of the pivot in the row above;
     - entries below each pivot are zero.
   REDUCED ROW ECHELON FORM (RREF): REF plus
     - every pivot equals 1;
     - each pivot is the only nonzero entry in its column.
   RREF of a matrix is UNIQUE; REF is not.
   Pivot columns = columns that contain pivots. Pivot variables
   (basic) correspond to pivot columns; FREE variables to non-pivot
   columns.
parts.F:
ALGORITHM (Gaussian elimination with back substitution)
     for each column left to right (the "pivot column"):
         pick a row (at or below the current row) with a non-zero entry in
         this column (partial pivoting: choose the largest |entry| for
         numerical stability); swap it up;
         use operation (3) to make all entries below the pivot zero.
     Then back-substitute from the last non-zero row upward.
     Gauss-Jordan elimination continues to RREF (also clears above the
     pivots and scales pivots to 1).
   Cost: about (2/3) n^3 floating-point operations for n x n: O(n^3).
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple (unique solution): solve
        x +  y +  z =  6
             2y + 5z = -4
        2x + 5y -  z = 27
     Augmented: [1 1 1 | 6 ; 0 2 5 | -4 ; 2 5 -1 | 27].
     R3 <- R3 - 2R1: [0 3 -3 | 15].
     R3 <- R3 - (3/2) R2: 3 - 3 = 0 for y; z: -3 - (3/2)(5) = -10.5;
        RHS: 15 - (3/2)(-4) = 21. So -10.5 z = 21 -> z = -2.
     Back: 2y + 5(-2) = -4 -> y = 3. x + 3 - 2 = 6 -> x = 5.
     Solution (5, 3, -2). Check eq.3: 10 + 15 + 2 = 27. OK.
   Moderate (infinitely many solutions): solve
        x + 2y + z = 4
        2x + 4y + 3z = 9
     [1 2 1 | 4 ; 2 4 3 | 9]; R2 <- R2 - 2R1: [0 0 1 | 1].
     z = 1; the first row gives x + 2y = 3. Pivot columns: 1 and 3.
     y is FREE: set y = t:  x = 3 - 2t, y = t, z = 1.
     Solution set: (3, 0, 1) + t(-2, 1, 0): a line in 3D.
   Moderate 2 (inconsistent):
        x + y = 2
        x + y = 3
     R2 <- R2 - R1: [0 0 | 1], i.e. 0 = 1: IMPOSSIBLE: no solution.
   Moderate 3 (RREF): [1 2 -1 | 3 ; 2 4 1 | 12]
     R2 <- R2 - 2R1: [0 0 3 | 6]; R2 <- R2/3: [0 0 1 | 2];
     R1 <- R1 + R2: [1 2 0 | 5]. RREF = [1 2 0 | 5 ; 0 0 1 | 2].
     x = 5 - 2y, z = 2, y free.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: the shape of RREF shows everything: pivot count =
   rank; free variables = n - rank = dimension of the family of
   solutions.

blocks.title: CLASSIFICATION OF SOLUTIONS (ROUCHE-CAPELLI / RANK CRITERION)
blocks.formulaBody:
For A x = b with A m x n and augmented matrix [A | b]:
     CONSISTENT (at least one solution) <=> rank(A) = rank([A | b]).
     If consistent and rank(A) = n (number of unknowns): UNIQUE solution.
     If consistent and rank(A) < n: INFINITELY many solutions, with
        n - rank(A) free parameters.
     If rank(A) < rank([A | b]): INCONSISTENT (a row 0 0 ... 0 | nonzero).

parts.B:
For A x = b with A m x n and augmented matrix [A | b]:
     CONSISTENT (at least one solution) <=> rank(A) = rank([A | b]).
     If consistent and rank(A) = n (number of unknowns): UNIQUE solution.
     If consistent and rank(A) < n: INFINITELY many solutions, with
        n - rank(A) free parameters.
     If rank(A) < rank([A | b]): INCONSISTENT (a row 0 0 ... 0 | nonzero).
parts.C: SYMBOLS: rank = number of pivots in REF.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: inconsistent means b is NOT in the column space of A; free
   variables mean some columns are redundant combinations of others.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS & SHAPE EXPECTATIONS (for any field of numbers)
     m < n  (fewer equations than unknowns): never a unique solution
            (either none or infinitely many).
     m = n and det(A) != 0: exactly one solution for every b.
     m > n  (overdetermined): usually inconsistent; use LEAST SQUARES
            (Module 10).
parts.G:
TABLE OF OUTCOMES
   rank(A) vs rank([A|b]) vs n         Result
   rank A < rank [A|b]                 no solution
   rank A = rank [A|b] = n             unique solution
   rank A = rank [A|b] < n             infinitely many (n - rank params)
parts.H:
Pivot-position test: a pivot in the augmented column signals
   inconsistency.
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: judging rank from the coefficient matrix only
   (compare with the augmented matrix); concluding 'unique solution'
   just because m = n without checking pivots.
parts.J:
RELATED: rank-nullity (F8.7), least squares for inconsistent systems
   (F10.5), homogeneous systems (F7.3).

     R3 <- R3 - (3/2) R2: 3 - 3 = 0 for y; z: -3 - (3/2)(5) = -10.5;
        RHS: 15 - (3/2)(-4) = 21. So -10.5 z = 21 -> z = -2.
     Back: 2y + 5(-2) = -4 -> y = 3. x + 3 - 2 = 6 -> x = 5.
     Solution (5, 3, -2). Check eq.3: 10 + 15 + 2 = 27. OK.
   Moderate (infinitely many solutions): solve
        x + 2y + z = 4
        2x + 4y + 3z = 9
     [1 2 1 | 4 ; 2 4 3 | 9]; R2 <- R2 - 2R1: [0 0 1 | 1].
     z = 1; the first row gives x + 2y = 3. Pivot columns: 1 and 3.
     y is FREE: set y = t:  x = 3 - 2t, y = t, z = 1.
     Solution set: (3, 0, 1) + t(-2, 1, 0): a line in 3D.
   Moderate 2 (inconsistent):
        x + y = 2
        x + y = 3
     R2 <- R2 - R1: [0 0 | 1], i.e. 0 = 1: IMPOSSIBLE: no solution.
   Moderate 3 (RREF): [1 2 -1 | 3 ; 2 4 1 | 12]
     R2 <- R2 - 2R1: [0 0 3 | 6]; R2 <- R2/3: [0 0 1 | 2];
     R1 <- R1 + R2: [1 2 0 | 5]. RREF = [1 2 0 | 5 ; 0 0 1 | 2].
     x = 5 - 2y, z = 2, y free.
H. INTERPRETATION: the shape of RREF shows everything: pivot count =
   rank; free variables = n - rank = dimension of the family of
   solutions.
I. MISTAKES: arithmetic slips (re-check by substituting); multiplying a
   row by 0; operating on only the coefficient side and not the RHS;
   dividing by a (near-)zero pivot without swapping rows.
J. RELATED: LU decomposition (A = LU, the matrix form of elimination;
   reuse for many right-hand sides) [SUPPLEMENTARY]; QR and Cholesky
   as alternatives for least squares (Module 10).

F7.2  CLASSIFICATION OF SOLUTIONS (ROUCHE-CAPELLI / RANK CRITERION)
B. For A x = b with A m x n and augmented matrix [A | b]:
     CONSISTENT (at least one solution) <=> rank(A) = rank([A | b]).
     If consistent and rank(A) = n (number of unknowns): UNIQUE solution.
     If consistent and rank(A) < n: INFINITELY many solutions, with
        n - rank(A) free parameters.
     If rank(A) < rank([A | b]): INCONSISTENT (a row 0 0 ... 0 | nonzero).
C. SYMBOLS: rank = number of pivots in REF.
D. CONCEPT: inconsistent means b is NOT in the column space of A; free
   variables mean some columns are redundant combinations of others.
E. CONDITIONS & SHAPE EXPECTATIONS (for any field of numbers)
     m < n  (fewer equations than unknowns): never a unique solution
            (either none or infinitely many).
     m = n and det(A) != 0: exactly one solution for every b.
     m > n  (overdetermined): usually inconsistent; use LEAST SQUARES
            (Module 10).
G. TABLE OF OUTCOMES
   rank(A) vs rank([A|b]) vs n         Result
   rank A < rank [A|b]                 no solution
   rank A = rank [A|b] = n             unique solution
   rank A = rank [A|b] < n             infinitely many (n - rank params)
H. Pivot-position test: a pivot in the augmented column signals
   inconsistency.
I. COMMON MISTAKES: judging rank from the coefficient matrix only
   (compare with the augmented matrix); concluding 'unique solution'
   just because m = n without checking pivots.
J. RELATED: rank-nullity (F8.7), least squares for inconsistent systems
   (F10.5), homogeneous systems (F7.3).

sections.title: HOMOGENEOUS SYSTEMS AND LINEAR COMBINATIONS OF SOLUTIONS

blocks.title: HOMOGENEOUS SYSTEM AND THE STRUCTURE OF SOLUTIONS
blocks.formulaBody:
/FACTS
   Homogeneous system: A x = 0 (right side all zeros).
     - ALWAYS consistent (the trivial solution x = 0).
     - Has non-trivial solutions <=> rank(A) < n (equivalently, there are
       free variables; columns of A are linearly dependent).
     - If m < n, non-trivial solutions always exist.
     - The solution set is the NULL SPACE of A (Module 8): closed under
       addition and scalar multiples: if Ax1 = 0 and Ax2 = 0 then
       A(c1 x1 + c2 x2) = 0.
   Non-homogeneous Ax = b with one particular solution x_p:
        EVERY solution is x = x_p + x_h, where x_h is any solution of
        A x = 0.
     (Proof: A(x - x_p) = b - b = 0.)

parts.A: NAME: Homogeneous system A x = 0; general solution x = x_p + x_h.
parts.B:
FORMULAS/FACTS
   Homogeneous system: A x = 0 (right side all zeros).
     - ALWAYS consistent (the trivial solution x = 0).
     - Has non-trivial solutions <=> rank(A) < n (equivalently, there are
       free variables; columns of A are linearly dependent).
     - If m < n, non-trivial solutions always exist.
     - The solution set is the NULL SPACE of A (Module 8): closed under
       addition and scalar multiples: if Ax1 = 0 and Ax2 = 0 then
       A(c1 x1 + c2 x2) = 0.
   Non-homogeneous Ax = b with one particular solution x_p:
        EVERY solution is x = x_p + x_h, where x_h is any solution of
        A x = 0.
     (Proof: A(x - x_p) = b - b = 0.)
parts.C: SYMBOLS: x_p particular solution; x_h homogeneous solution.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the solution set is a translate of the null space: a line,
   plane or higher-dimensional flat, not through the origin unless b = 0.
   This is the linear-algebra analog of "general solution = particular
   solution + complementary function" in differential equations
   (Module 15).
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: the structure x = x_p + x_h holds when Ax = b is
   consistent; x_h ranges over the whole null space of A.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: x + 2y + z = 4 and 2x + 4y + 3z = 9 (from F7.1): x_p = (3,0,1);
        homogeneous part: x + 2y + z = 0 and 2x + 4y + 3z = 0 ->
        z = 0, x = -2y: x_h = t(-2, 1, 0). General solution
        (3,0,1) + t(-2,1,0).
   Moderate: solve  x + y + z = 0;  2x - y + 3z = 0;  x - 2y + 2z = 0.
        Augmented: [1 1 1 ; 2 -1 3 ; 1 -2 2] (rhs zero).
        R2 <- R2 - 2R1: [0 -3 1]; R3 <- R3 - R1: [0 -3 1].
        R3 <- R3 - R2: [0 0 0]. Rank 2 < 3: one free variable.
        -3y + z = 0 -> z = 3y; x = -y - z = -4y. With y = t:
        x = t(-4, 1, 3). Check eq.2: 2(-4) - 1 + 9 = 0. OK.
        Non-trivial solutions exist; the null space is the line through
        (-4, 1, 3).
   Linear combination of solutions: if (-4,1,3) is a solution, so is
        5(-4,1,3) = (-20, 5, 15).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: non-trivial solutions of A x = 0 mean redundancy among
   the columns: they are exactly the linear dependencies. In regression,
   a non-trivial null space of X means perfectly collinear predictors
   (X^T X is singular; coefficients are not unique).
parts.I:
MISTAKES: forgetting that a homogeneous system always has the
   trivial solution; declaring "no solution".
parts.J:
RELATED: null space, rank-nullity theorem (Module 8); eigenvectors
   solve (A - lambda I) x = 0 (Module 9).

sections.title: PYTHON AND NUMERICAL NOTES (SOLVING SYSTEMS IN PRACTICE)

blocks.rawText:
import numpy as np
    A = np.array([[1., 1., 1.], [0., 2., 5.], [2., 5., -1.]])
    b = np.array([6., -4., 27.])
    x = np.linalg.solve(A, b)        # [ 5.  3. -2.]
    rank = np.linalg.matrix_rank(A)  # 3
    # Overdetermined / rank-deficient: least squares
    x_ls, res, rk, sv = np.linalg.lstsq(A, b, rcond=None)
  Notes: np.linalg.solve uses LU with partial pivoting. Floating-point
  arithmetic means rank decisions use tolerances: a pivot of 1e-17 is
  treated as zero. Condition number cond(A) = sigma_max/sigma_min tells
  how much errors in b can be amplified in x; cond > 1e8-1e12 means
  results are unreliable in double precision.

MINI REFERENCE: HOW MANY SOLUTIONS? FAST CHECKLIST
   1. Write [A | b]; row reduce.
   2. A row [0 ... 0 | c] with c != 0?  -> no solution.
   3. Otherwise count pivots r. r = n -> unique. r < n -> infinite,
      n - r free variables.
   4. Square case: det(A) != 0 <=> unique solution for every b.
