sections.title: CIRCLES, SPHERES AND QUADRATIC SURFACES

blocks.title: CIRCLE AND SPHERE
blocks.formulaBody:
Circle: (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2   (center (h, k), radius r).
   Sphere: (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 + (z - l)^2 = r^2.
   General: x^2 + y^2 + D x + E y + F = 0 -> complete the square.

parts.B:
Circle: (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2   (center (h, k), radius r).
   Sphere: (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 + (z - l)^2 = r^2.
   General: x^2 + y^2 + D x + E y + F = 0 -> complete the square.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: (h, k) and (h, k, l) the center; r > 0 the radius; D, E, F
   the coefficients of the general form.
parts.D: CONCEPT: all points at the constant distance r from the center.
parts.E:
If the right-hand side after completing the square is <= 0, there is no
   circle (a single point or empty set).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: level sets of squared distance; L2 balls
   (regularization constraints) are discs or spheres.
parts.I: MISTAKE: forgetting to add the completed-square terms to BOTH sides.
parts.J:
RELATED: distance formula (F11.1), completing the square (F1.8),
   ellipsoids (F11.6).

blocks.rawText:
F11.5  CIRCLE AND SPHERE
B. Circle: (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2   (center (h, k), radius r).
   Sphere: (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 + (z - l)^2 = r^2.
   General: x^2 + y^2 + D x + E y + F = 0 -> complete the square.
C. SYMBOLS: (h, k) and (h, k, l) the center; r > 0 the radius; D, E, F
   the coefficients of the general form.
D. CONCEPT: all points at the constant distance r from the center.
G. EXAMPLES
   Circle: x^2 + y^2 - 6x + 4y - 12 = 0 -> (x^2 - 6x + 9) + (y^2 + 4y + 4)
        = 12 + 9 + 4 -> (x - 3)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 25: center (3, -2),
        radius 5.
   Sphere: x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 2x + 4y - 6z = -5 -> (x-1)^2 + (y+2)^2 +
        (z-3)^2 = -5 + 1 + 4 + 9 = 9: center (1, -2, 3), radius 3.
E. If the right-hand side after completing the square is <= 0, there is no
   circle (a single point or empty set).
H. INTERPRETATION: level sets of squared distance; L2 balls
   (regularization constraints) are discs or spheres.
I. MISTAKE: forgetting to add the completed-square terms to BOTH sides.
J. RELATED: distance formula (F11.1), completing the square (F1.8),
   ellipsoids (F11.6).

blocks.title: QUADRIC SURFACES (second-degree surfaces)
blocks.formulaBody:
STANDARD FORMS (centered at the origin, axes aligned; a, b, c > 0)
   Ellipsoid:            x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 + z^2/c^2 = 1
   Hyperboloid, 1 sheet: x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 - z^2/c^2 = 1
   Hyperboloid, 2 sheets: -x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 + z^2/c^2 = 1
   Elliptic paraboloid:  z = x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2          (a bowl)
   Hyperbolic paraboloid: z = x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2          (a saddle)
   Elliptic cone:        z^2 = x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2
   Cylinders: an equation MISSING one variable (e.g. x^2 + y^2 = r^2 is a
     circular cylinder along the z-axis; z = x^2 is a parabolic cylinder
     along the y-axis).

parts.B:
STANDARD FORMS (centered at the origin, axes aligned; a, b, c > 0)
   Ellipsoid:            x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 + z^2/c^2 = 1
   Hyperboloid, 1 sheet: x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 - z^2/c^2 = 1
   Hyperboloid, 2 sheets: -x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 + z^2/c^2 = 1
   Elliptic paraboloid:  z = x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2          (a bowl)
   Hyperbolic paraboloid: z = x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2          (a saddle)
   Elliptic cone:        z^2 = x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2
   Cylinders: an equation MISSING one variable (e.g. x^2 + y^2 = r^2 is a
     circular cylinder along the z-axis; z = x^2 is a parabolic cylinder
     along the y-axis).
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: a, b, c > 0 the semi-axis lengths or scale parameters; x, y,
   z the coordinates.
parts.D:
HOW TO RECOGNIZE A SURFACE: take TRACES, i.e. set one variable constant
   and look at the 2D curve.
   Paraboloid z = x^2 + y^2: z = k > 0 gives circles; x = 0 gives the
   parabola z = y^2.
   Saddle z = x^2 - y^2: along x = 0, z = -y^2 (opens down); along y = 0,
   z = x^2 (opens up).
parts.G:
EXAMPLE: 4x^2 + 9y^2 + 36 z^2 = 36 -> divide by 36: x^2/9 + y^2/4 + z^2
   = 1: ellipsoid with semi-axes 3 (x), 2 (y), 1 (z).
parts.H:
DATA SCIENCE LINK: quadratic loss surfaces are paraboloids; the saddle
   shape is what the optimizer meets at saddle points; confidence
   regions of a multivariate normal are ellipsoids (Mahalanobis distance
   = constant gives ellipsoids x^T Sigma^(-1) x = c).
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: confusing the one-sheet and two-sheet hyperboloids
   (sign pattern); forgetting that a missing variable gives a cylinder.
parts.J:
RELATED: Hessian classification (Module 12): quadratic form types

blocks.rawText:
F11.6  QUADRIC SURFACES (second-degree surfaces)
B. STANDARD FORMS (centered at the origin, axes aligned; a, b, c > 0)
   Ellipsoid:            x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 + z^2/c^2 = 1
   Hyperboloid, 1 sheet: x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 - z^2/c^2 = 1
   Hyperboloid, 2 sheets: -x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 + z^2/c^2 = 1
   Elliptic paraboloid:  z = x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2          (a bowl)
   Hyperbolic paraboloid: z = x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2          (a saddle)
   Elliptic cone:        z^2 = x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2
   Cylinders: an equation MISSING one variable (e.g. x^2 + y^2 = r^2 is a
     circular cylinder along the z-axis; z = x^2 is a parabolic cylinder
     along the y-axis).
C. SYMBOLS: a, b, c > 0 the semi-axis lengths or scale parameters; x, y,
   z the coordinates.
D. HOW TO RECOGNIZE A SURFACE: take TRACES, i.e. set one variable constant
   and look at the 2D curve.
   Paraboloid z = x^2 + y^2: z = k > 0 gives circles; x = 0 gives the
   parabola z = y^2.
   Saddle z = x^2 - y^2: along x = 0, z = -y^2 (opens down); along y = 0,
   z = x^2 (opens up).
E. CONDITIONS: these are the standard (centered, axis-aligned) forms;
   general quadrics need rotation and translation (eigen-decomposition
   of the quadratic form, F9.4).
G. EXAMPLE: 4x^2 + 9y^2 + 36 z^2 = 36 -> divide by 36: x^2/9 + y^2/4 + z^2
   = 1: ellipsoid with semi-axes 3 (x), 2 (y), 1 (z).
H. DATA SCIENCE LINK: quadratic loss surfaces are paraboloids; the saddle
   shape is what the optimizer meets at saddle points; confidence
   regions of a multivariate normal are ellipsoids (Mahalanobis distance
   = constant gives ellipsoids x^T Sigma^(-1) x = c).
I. COMMON MISTAKES: confusing the one-sheet and two-sheet hyperboloids
   (sign pattern); forgetting that a missing variable gives a cylinder.
J. RELATED: Hessian classification (Module 12): quadratic form types
   (PD -> paraboloid bowl, indefinite -> saddle) correspond to these
   surfaces.

sections.rawText:
F11.5  CIRCLE AND SPHERE
B. Circle: (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2   (center (h, k), radius r).
   Sphere: (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 + (z - l)^2 = r^2.
   General: x^2 + y^2 + D x + E y + F = 0 -> complete the square.
C. SYMBOLS: (h, k) and (h, k, l) the center; r > 0 the radius; D, E, F
   the coefficients of the general form.
D. CONCEPT: all points at the constant distance r from the center.
G. EXAMPLES
   Circle: x^2 + y^2 - 6x + 4y - 12 = 0 -> (x^2 - 6x + 9) + (y^2 + 4y + 4)
        = 12 + 9 + 4 -> (x - 3)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 25: center (3, -2),
        radius 5.
   Sphere: x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 2x + 4y - 6z = -5 -> (x-1)^2 + (y+2)^2 +
        (z-3)^2 = -5 + 1 + 4 + 9 = 9: center (1, -2, 3), radius 3.

   circle (a single point or empty set).
H. INTERPRETATION: level sets of squared distance; L2 balls
   (regularization constraints) are discs or spheres.
I. MISTAKE: forgetting to add the completed-square terms to BOTH sides.
J. RELATED: distance formula (F11.1), completing the square (F1.8),
   ellipsoids (F11.6).

sections.title: FUNCTIONS OF SEVERAL VARIABLES; DOMAIN, RANGE, LEVEL CURVES

blocks.rawText:
BASIC IDEA: Many quantities depend on more than one input: house price
depends on area, location, age; a model's loss depends on all its
weights. A function of two variables f(x, y) assigns one number z to
each point (x, y): its graph is a SURFACE in 3D.
   f : R^n -> R  (scalar field);  f : R^n -> R^m (vector-valued).
DOMAIN: set of allowed input points (apply the same rules as Module 1.4:
   denominators, roots, logs). Example f(x,y) = ln(x + y - 1)/sqrt(y - x^2):
   need x + y > 1 and y > x^2.
RANGE: the set of attained outputs.
LEVEL CURVES (CONTOURS): the set {(x,y) : f(x,y) = c}. Like a topographic
   map: each curve joins points of equal height. Closely spaced contours
   mean steep slope. For f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2 the contours are concentric
   circles; for f = x^2 + 4y^2 they are ellipses (flatter along x);
   for f = x^2 - y^2 they are hyperbolas.
LEVEL SURFACES: f(x,y,z) = c in 3D.

sections.title: PARTIAL DERIVATIVES

blocks.title: PARTIAL DERIVATIVE
blocks.formulaBody:
df/dx = f_x(x, y) = lim[h -> 0] ( f(x + h, y) - f(x, y) ) / h
     df/dy = f_y(x, y) = lim[h -> 0] ( f(x, y + h) - f(x, y) ) / h
   (written with the curly "partial" symbol in print: PARTIAL f/PARTIAL x.)
   Rule: differentiate with respect to ONE variable while treating all the
   others as constants.

parts.B:
FORMULA
     df/dx = f_x(x, y) = lim[h -> 0] ( f(x + h, y) - f(x, y) ) / h
     df/dy = f_y(x, y) = lim[h -> 0] ( f(x, y + h) - f(x, y) ) / h
   (written with the curly "partial" symbol in print: PARTIAL f/PARTIAL x.)
   Rule: differentiate with respect to ONE variable while treating all the
   others as constants.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: f_x means "partial derivative of f with respect to x"; h a small
   change in ONE variable only.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the slope of the surface in the x-direction (holding y fixed): the
   slope of the cross-section curve. It measures the sensitivity of f to
   one input, everything else held constant.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: f must be defined near the point; existence of both
   partials at a point does NOT guarantee that f is continuous there
   (different from the single-variable case); differentiability needs
   continuous partials (sufficient).
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: f(x, y) = x^2 y + 3 x y^2 - y^3.
        f_x = 2xy + 3y^2;  f_y = x^2 + 6xy - 3y^2.
        At (1, 2): f_x = 4 + 12 = 16; f_y = 1 + 12 - 12 = 1.
   Moderate: f(x, y) = e^(x y) sin(y): f_x = y e^(xy) sin y;
        f_y = x e^(xy) sin y + e^(xy) cos y (product + chain rule).
   Moderate 2 (data science): MSE for a model y_hat = w x + b over one
        point: L(w, b) = (w x + b - y)^2:
        dL/dw = 2 (w x + b - y) x;  dL/db = 2 (w x + b - y).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: f_x(1, 2) = 16: moving from (1,2) in the +x direction
   by 0.01 raises f by about 0.16 if y is held fixed.
parts.J: RELATED: gradient (F12.3), chain rule (F12.5).

blocks.title: HIGHER-ORDER PARTIAL DERIVATIVES AND CLAIRAUT'S THEOREM
blocks.formulaBody:
f_xx = d/dx(f_x); f_yy; mixed: f_xy = d/dy(f_x) [differentiate first in x,
   then in y] and f_yx.
   CLAIRAUT'S (SCHWARZ'S) THEOREM: if f_xy and f_yx are continuous near
   the point, then f_xy = f_yx.
   NOTATION WARNING: some books write f_xy for "first x then y", others
   for the reverse. This document: f_xy = (f_x)_y.

parts.B:
f_xx = d/dx(f_x); f_yy; mixed: f_xy = d/dy(f_x) [differentiate first in x,
   then in y] and f_yx.
   CLAIRAUT'S (SCHWARZ'S) THEOREM: if f_xy and f_yx are continuous near
   the point, then f_xy = f_yx.
   NOTATION WARNING: some books write f_xy for "first x then y", others
   for the reverse. This document: f_xy = (f_x)_y.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: f_xx the second partial in x; f_xy = (f_x)_y the mixed
   partial; continuity of these partials is required.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: Clairaut needs f_xy and f_yx continuous near the point;
   counterexamples exist otherwise.
parts.G:
EXAMPLE: f = x^3 y^2: f_x = 3x^2 y^2; f_xy = 6 x^2 y; f_y = 2 x^3 y;
   f_yx = 6 x^2 y. Equal.
parts.D:
WHY IT MATTERS: the Hessian matrix of a nice function is symmetric
   (F12.6).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: curvature in each direction, and how the slope in x
   changes as y changes; makes the Hessian symmetric.
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: mixing up the order convention; assuming symmetry
   without continuity.
parts.J: RELATED: Hessian (F12.6), second-order optimization (F43.4).

sections.title: GRADIENT VECTORS AND DIRECTIONAL DERIVATIVES

blocks.title: GRADIENT
blocks.formulaBody:
grad f = (f_x, f_y)   for f(x, y);   in general
     grad f(x) = ( df/dx1, df/dx2, ..., df/dxn )^T   (column vector)
   Notation: nabla f, with nabla = "del".

parts.B:
FORMULA
     grad f = (f_x, f_y)   for f(x, y);   in general
     grad f(x) = ( df/dx1, df/dx2, ..., df/dxn )^T   (column vector)
   Notation: nabla f, with nabla = "del".
parts.C: SYMBOLS: x = (x1, ..., xn); each component is a partial derivative.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the gradient is a vector that POINTS in the direction of
   steepest ascent of f, and its length |grad f| is the steepest rate of
   increase. It is PERPENDICULAR to the level curve/surface through the
   point. The negative gradient is the direction of steepest descent;
   this is the foundation of gradient descent (Module 43).
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: f differentiable at the point. grad f = 0 at a critical
   point.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: f = x^2 + y^2: grad f = (2x, 2y), pointing radially outward
        from the origin; perpendicular to the circular level curves.
   Moderate: f(x, y) = x^2 y + 3 x y^2 - y^3 at (1, 2): grad f = (16, 1).
        Steepest ascent direction (16, 1)/sqrt(257); max rate of change
        sqrt(257) = 16.03.
   Level-curve normal: for x^2 + 4 y^2 = 8 at (2, 1): grad = (2x, 8y) =
        (4, 8): the tangent to the ellipse has direction (8, -4)
        (perpendicular to the gradient) with slope -1/2. (Same as
        implicit differentiation: dy/dx = -f_x/f_y = -4/8 = -1/2.)
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: gradient ascent moves along grad f, descent along
   -grad f; the gradient magnitude is the steepness.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: treating the gradient as a scalar; computing it at the wrong
   point; confusing "gradient" (vector of partials of a scalar function)
   with the Jacobian (matrix of partials of a vector function).
parts.J:
RELATED: directional derivative (F12.4); gradient descent
   w <- w - eta grad L(w).

blocks.title: DIRECTIONAL DERIVATIVE
blocks.formulaBody:
D_u f(a) = grad f(a) . u = |grad f(a)| cos(theta), where u is a UNIT
   vector and theta the angle between u and the gradient.

parts.B:
D_u f(a) = grad f(a) . u = |grad f(a)| cos(theta), where u is a UNIT
   vector and theta the angle between u and the gradient.
parts.C: SYMBOLS: u unit direction vector (|u| = 1).
parts.D:
CONCEPT: rate of change of f when moving from a in the direction u.
   Largest (= |grad f|) when u points along the gradient (theta = 0);
   zero along level curves (theta = 90 deg); most negative (-|grad f|) in
   the opposite direction.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: u must have length 1; if given a non-unit vector, divide
   by its length first.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: the slope of the surface when walking in direction u;
   largest along the gradient (value |grad f|), zero along level curves.
parts.I: MISTAKE: forgetting to normalize the direction vector.
parts.J:
RELATED: gradient (F12.3), chain rule (F12.5), gradient descent
   (F43.2).

blocks.rawText:
F12.4  DIRECTIONAL DERIVATIVE
B. D_u f(a) = grad f(a) . u = |grad f(a)| cos(theta), where u is a UNIT
   vector and theta the angle between u and the gradient.
C. SYMBOLS: u unit direction vector (|u| = 1).
D. CONCEPT: rate of change of f when moving from a in the direction u.
   Largest (= |grad f|) when u points along the gradient (theta = 0);
   zero along level curves (theta = 90 deg); most negative (-|grad f|) in
   the opposite direction.
E. CONDITIONS: u must have length 1; if given a non-unit vector, divide
   by its length first.
G. EXAMPLE: f = x^2 y + 3 x y^2 - y^3 at (1, 2), direction (3, 4):
   u = (3, 4)/5 = (0.6, 0.8). D_u f = (16)(0.6) + (1)(0.8) = 9.6 + 0.8
   = 10.4.
H. INTERPRETATION: the slope of the surface when walking in direction u;
   largest along the gradient (value |grad f|), zero along level curves.
I. MISTAKE: forgetting to normalize the direction vector.
J. RELATED: gradient (F12.3), chain rule (F12.5), gradient descent
   (F43.2).

sections.rawText:
F12.3  GRADIENT
A. NAME: Gradient.
B. FORMULA
     grad f = (f_x, f_y)   for f(x, y);   in general
     grad f(x) = ( df/dx1, df/dx2, ..., df/dxn )^T   (column vector)
   Notation: nabla f, with nabla = "del".
C. SYMBOLS: x = (x1, ..., xn); each component is a partial derivative.
D. CONCEPT: the gradient is a vector that POINTS in the direction of
   steepest ascent of f, and its length |grad f| is the steepest rate of
   increase. It is PERPENDICULAR to the level curve/surface through the
   point. The negative gradient is the direction of steepest descent;
   this is the foundation of gradient descent (Module 43).
E. CONDITIONS: f differentiable at the point. grad f = 0 at a critical
   point.
G. EXAMPLES
   Simple: f = x^2 + y^2: grad f = (2x, 2y), pointing radially outward
        from the origin; perpendicular to the circular level curves.
   Moderate: f(x, y) = x^2 y + 3 x y^2 - y^3 at (1, 2): grad f = (16, 1).
        Steepest ascent direction (16, 1)/sqrt(257); max rate of change
        sqrt(257) = 16.03.
   Level-curve normal: for x^2 + 4 y^2 = 8 at (2, 1): grad = (2x, 8y) =
        (4, 8): the tangent to the ellipse has direction (8, -4)
        (perpendicular to the gradient) with slope -1/2. (Same as
        implicit differentiation: dy/dx = -f_x/f_y = -4/8 = -1/2.)
H. INTERPRETATION: gradient ascent moves along grad f, descent along
   -grad f; the gradient magnitude is the steepness.
I. MISTAKES: treating the gradient as a scalar; computing it at the wrong
   point; confusing "gradient" (vector of partials of a scalar function)
   with the Jacobian (matrix of partials of a vector function).
J. RELATED: directional derivative (F12.4); gradient descent
   w <- w - eta grad L(w).

F12.4  DIRECTIONAL DERIVATIVE
B. D_u f(a) = grad f(a) . u = |grad f(a)| cos(theta), where u is a UNIT
   vector and theta the angle between u and the gradient.
C. SYMBOLS: u unit direction vector (|u| = 1).
D. CONCEPT: rate of change of f when moving from a in the direction u.
   Largest (= |grad f|) when u points along the gradient (theta = 0);
   zero along level curves (theta = 90 deg); most negative (-|grad f|) in
   the opposite direction.
E. CONDITIONS: u must have length 1; if given a non-unit vector, divide
   by its length first.
G. EXAMPLE: f = x^2 y + 3 x y^2 - y^3 at (1, 2), direction (3, 4):
   u = (3, 4)/5 = (0.6, 0.8). D_u f = (16)(0.6) + (1)(0.8) = 9.6 + 0.8
   = 10.4.
H. INTERPRETATION: the slope of the surface when walking in direction u;
   largest along the gradient (value |grad f|), zero along level curves.
I. MISTAKE: forgetting to normalize the direction vector.
J. RELATED: gradient (F12.3), chain rule (F12.5), gradient descent
   (F43.2).

sections.title: CHAIN RULE FOR MULTIVARIABLE FUNCTIONS

blocks.title: MULTIVARIABLE CHAIN RULE
blocks.formulaBody:
If z = f(x, y), x = x(t), y = y(t):
         dz/dt = f_x dx/dt + f_y dy/dt = grad f . (dx/dt, dy/dt).
     If x = x(s, t), y = y(s, t):
         dz/ds = f_x x_s + f_y y_s;   dz/dt = f_x x_t + f_y y_t.
     General: for y = f(g(x)) with g: R^n -> R^m, f: R^m -> R:
         grad_x y = J_g(x)^T grad f(g(x)),
     where J_g is the Jacobian matrix (m x n) of g.

parts.B:

parts.D:
CONCEPT: sum over ALL paths through which t influences z. This is

parts.E: CONDITIONS: f differentiable (continuous partials suffice).

   back-propagation applies this rule layer by layer.

sections.title: CRITICAL POINTS, THE HESSIAN, AND CLASSIFICATION

blocks.title: CRITICAL POINTS AND THE HESSIAN MATRIX
blocks.formulaBody:
Critical (stationary) point: grad f(a) = 0 (all partial derivatives 0)
        or a partial derivative does not exist.
     Hessian matrix H (n x n): H_ij = d^2 f / (dx_i dx_j). For two variables
        H = [ f_xx  f_xy ; f_yx  f_yy ]  (symmetric if Clairaut applies).
     Second-derivative test for f(x, y) at a critical point (a, b):
        D = det H = f_xx f_yy - (f_xy)^2   evaluated at (a, b).
          D > 0 and f_xx > 0  -> LOCAL MINIMUM
          D > 0 and f_xx < 0  -> LOCAL MAXIMUM
          D < 0               -> SADDLE POINT
          D = 0               -> inconclusive.
     General n-variable version (H symmetric at a critical point):
          H positive definite (all eigenvalues > 0)   -> local minimum
          H negative definite (all eigenvalues < 0)   -> local maximum
          H indefinite (eigenvalues of both signs)    -> saddle
          H singular (some eigenvalue 0)              -> inconclusive.
     Second-order Taylor expansion:
        f(a + h) approx f(a) + grad f(a)^T h + (1/2) h^T H(a) h.

parts.A: NAME: Critical points; Hessian; second-derivative test.
parts.B:
FORMULAS
     Critical (stationary) point: grad f(a) = 0 (all partial derivatives 0)
        or a partial derivative does not exist.
     Hessian matrix H (n x n): H_ij = d^2 f / (dx_i dx_j). For two variables
        H = [ f_xx  f_xy ; f_yx  f_yy ]  (symmetric if Clairaut applies).
     Second-derivative test for f(x, y) at a critical point (a, b):
        D = det H = f_xx f_yy - (f_xy)^2   evaluated at (a, b).
          D > 0 and f_xx > 0  -> LOCAL MINIMUM
          D > 0 and f_xx < 0  -> LOCAL MAXIMUM
          D < 0               -> SADDLE POINT
          D = 0               -> inconclusive.
     General n-variable version (H symmetric at a critical point):
          H positive definite (all eigenvalues > 0)   -> local minimum
          H negative definite (all eigenvalues < 0)   -> local maximum
          H indefinite (eigenvalues of both signs)    -> saddle
          H singular (some eigenvalue 0)              -> inconclusive.
     Second-order Taylor expansion:
        f(a + h) approx f(a) + grad f(a)^T h + (1/2) h^T H(a) h.
parts.C: SYMBOLS: f_xx second partial in x; f_xy mixed; h a small step vector.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: at a critical point the first-order term vanishes, so the
   behavior is governed by the quadratic form h^T H h (Module 9.6):
   positive in every direction -> bowl (min); negative -> dome (max);
   mixed -> saddle (up in some directions, down in others).
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: continuous second partials. Critical points are only
   candidates; for GLOBAL extremes also examine the boundary and behavior
   at infinity. (On a closed bounded region: evaluate on the boundary as
   well; EVT, F2.7.)
parts.F:
DERIVATION: use the Taylor expansion above with grad f = 0.
   In 2D: h^T H h = f_xx h1^2 + 2 f_xy h1 h2 + f_yy h2^2; completing the
   square shows sign depends on f_xx and D.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: f(x, y) = x^2 + x y + y^2. grad = (2x + y, x + 2y) = 0 only at
        (0, 0). H = [2 1 ; 1 2]; D = 4 - 1 = 3 > 0, f_xx = 2 > 0: minimum
        (eigenvalues 3 and 1, both positive).
   Moderate: f(x, y) = x^3 - 3x + y^2 - 2y.
        f_x = 3x^2 - 3 = 0 -> x = +/- 1;  f_y = 2y - 2 = 0 -> y = 1.
        Critical points (1, 1) and (-1, 1).
        f_xx = 6x, f_yy = 2, f_xy = 0: D = 12 x.
        At (1, 1): D = 12 > 0, f_xx = 6 > 0: LOCAL MIN, f = 1 - 3 + 1 - 2
        = -3.
        At (-1, 1): D = -12 < 0: SADDLE, f = -1 + 3 + 1 - 2 = 1.
   Moderate 2 (saddle): f = x^2 - y^2: critical point (0,0); H =
        diag(2, -2); D = -4 < 0: saddle.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: In deep learning most critical points in high dimension
   are saddles, not local minima; eigenvalues of the Hessian give the
   curvature in each principal direction; the ratio largest/smallest
   eigenvalue (condition number) controls how hard the problem is.
parts.J:
RELATED: second-derivative test in one variable (F3.14) is the 1D
   special case; Newton's method uses H^(-1) (Module 43); Lagrange
   multipliers (below).

blocks.title: TANGENT PLANE AND LINEARIZATION  [multivariable version of F3.2]
blocks.formulaBody:
z approx f(a, b) + f_x(a, b)(x - a) + f_y(a, b)(y - b).
   In vector form: f(x) approx f(a) + grad f(a)^T (x - a).

parts.B:
z approx f(a, b) + f_x(a, b)(x - a) + f_y(a, b)(y - b).
   In vector form: f(x) approx f(a) + grad f(a)^T (x - a).
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: (a, b) the base point; f_x(a, b), f_y(a, b) the partial
   derivatives there; x - a, y - b the steps.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: near (a, b) the surface looks like its tangent plane; the
   linearization predicts small changes by adding the partial effects.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: f differentiable at (a, b); accurate only for small steps
   (error is second order, about (1/2) h^T H h).
parts.H: INTERPRETATION: sensitivity analysis: df is about f_x dx + f_y dy.
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: using it far from (a, b); forgetting that it is the
   first-order Taylor polynomial.
parts.J:
RELATED: tangent line (F3.2), Taylor series (F5.6), second-order
   expansion (F12.6).

blocks.title: CONSTRAINED OPTIMIZATION: LAGRANGE MULTIPLIERS [SUPPLEMENTARY]
blocks.formulaBody:
To optimize f(x) subject to g(x) = 0: solve grad f = lambda grad g with
   g(x) = 0. lambda is the Lagrange multiplier (shadow price).

parts.B:
To optimize f(x) subject to g(x) = 0: solve grad f = lambda grad g with
   g(x) = 0. lambda is the Lagrange multiplier (shadow price).
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: f the objective; g the constraint; lambda the Lagrange
   multiplier.
parts.D:
At a constrained optimum the level curve of f is tangent to the
   constraint curve, so their normals (gradients) are parallel.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: needs grad g != 0 at the optimum (regularity); it gives
   candidates, which must be checked as maxima or minima; inequality
   constraints need KKT (Appendix D).
parts.G:
EXAMPLE: maximize x y subject to x + y = 10: grad f = (y, x) = lambda
   (1, 1) -> x = y = 5, f = 25.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: lambda measures how much the optimal value changes
   per unit relaxation of the constraint (shadow price).
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: forgetting to impose g = 0 together with the
   gradient equations; not checking whether a candidate is a maximum or
   a minimum.
parts.J:
RELATED: PCA (maximize v^T S v subject to |v| = 1 gives S v = lambda v),
   SVM and regularization as constrained problems (Module 48), KKT
   conditions (Appendix D).

GRADIENT-DESCENT MICRO EXAMPLE: f(x, y) = x^2 + 3 y^2, start (2, 1),
learning rate eta = 0.1: grad f = (2x, 6y) = (4, 6); new point
(2 - 0.4, 1 - 0.6) = (1.6, 0.4); f falls from 7 to 2.56 + 0.48 = 3.04.

        f(a + h) approx f(a) + grad f(a)^T h + (1/2) h^T H(a) h.

D. CONCEPT: at a critical point the first-order term vanishes, so the
   behavior is governed by the quadratic form h^T H h (Module 9.6):
   positive in every direction -> bowl (min); negative -> dome (max);
   mixed -> saddle (up in some directions, down in others).
E. CONDITIONS: continuous second partials. Critical points are only
   candidates; for GLOBAL extremes also examine the boundary and behavior
   at infinity. (On a closed bounded region: evaluate on the boundary as
   well; EVT, F2.7.)
F. DERIVATION: use the Taylor expansion above with grad f = 0.
   In 2D: h^T H h = f_xx h1^2 + 2 f_xy h1 h2 + f_yy h2^2; completing the
   square shows sign depends on f_xx and D.
G. EXAMPLES
   Simple: f(x, y) = x^2 + x y + y^2. grad = (2x + y, x + 2y) = 0 only at
        (0, 0). H = [2 1 ; 1 2]; D = 4 - 1 = 3 > 0, f_xx = 2 > 0: minimum
        (eigenvalues 3 and 1, both positive).
   Moderate: f(x, y) = x^3 - 3x + y^2 - 2y.
        f_x = 3x^2 - 3 = 0 -> x = +/- 1;  f_y = 2y - 2 = 0 -> y = 1.
        Critical points (1, 1) and (-1, 1).
        f_xx = 6x, f_yy = 2, f_xy = 0: D = 12 x.
        At (1, 1): D = 12 > 0, f_xx = 6 > 0: LOCAL MIN, f = 1 - 3 + 1 - 2
        = -3.
        At (-1, 1): D = -12 < 0: SADDLE, f = -1 + 3 + 1 - 2 = 1.
   Moderate 2 (saddle): f = x^2 - y^2: critical point (0,0); H =
        diag(2, -2); D = -4 < 0: saddle.
H. INTERPRETATION: In deep learning most critical points in high dimension
   are saddles, not local minima; eigenvalues of the Hessian give the
   curvature in each principal direction; the ratio largest/smallest
   eigenvalue (condition number) controls how hard the problem is.
I. MISTAKES: forgetting to compute D at the specific point; using
   f_xx f_yy instead of f_xx f_yy - f_xy^2; claiming a max/min when D = 0;
   ignoring the boundary for global extremes.
J. RELATED: second-derivative test in one variable (F3.14) is the 1D
   special case; Newton's method uses H^(-1) (Module 43); Lagrange
   multipliers (below).

F12.7  TANGENT PLANE AND LINEARIZATION  [multivariable version of F3.2]
B. z approx f(a, b) + f_x(a, b)(x - a) + f_y(a, b)(y - b).
   In vector form: f(x) approx f(a) + grad f(a)^T (x - a).
C. SYMBOLS: (a, b) the base point; f_x(a, b), f_y(a, b) the partial
   derivatives there; x - a, y - b the steps.
D. CONCEPT: near (a, b) the surface looks like its tangent plane; the
   linearization predicts small changes by adding the partial effects.
E. CONDITIONS: f differentiable at (a, b); accurate only for small steps
   (error is second order, about (1/2) h^T H h).
G. EXAMPLE: f = x^2 y at (2, 1): f = 4, f_x = 4, f_y = 4. Estimate
   f(2.1, 0.9): 4 + 4(0.1) + 4(-0.1) = 4.0 (true: 0.9 * 4.41 = 3.969).
H. INTERPRETATION: sensitivity analysis: df is about f_x dx + f_y dy.
I. COMMON MISTAKES: using it far from (a, b); forgetting that it is the
   first-order Taylor polynomial.
J. RELATED: tangent line (F3.2), Taylor series (F5.6), second-order
   expansion (F12.6).

F12.8  CONSTRAINED OPTIMIZATION: LAGRANGE MULTIPLIERS [SUPPLEMENTARY]
B. To optimize f(x) subject to g(x) = 0: solve grad f = lambda grad g with
   g(x) = 0. lambda is the Lagrange multiplier (shadow price).
C. SYMBOLS: f the objective; g the constraint; lambda the Lagrange
   multiplier.
D. At a constrained optimum the level curve of f is tangent to the
   constraint curve, so their normals (gradients) are parallel.
E. CONDITIONS: needs grad g != 0 at the optimum (regularity); it gives
   candidates, which must be checked as maxima or minima; inequality
   constraints need KKT (Appendix D).
G. EXAMPLE: maximize x y subject to x + y = 10: grad f = (y, x) = lambda
   (1, 1) -> x = y = 5, f = 25.
H. INTERPRETATION: lambda measures how much the optimal value changes
   per unit relaxation of the constraint (shadow price).
I. COMMON MISTAKES: forgetting to impose g = 0 together with the
   gradient equations; not checking whether a candidate is a maximum or
   a minimum.
J. RELATED: PCA (maximize v^T S v subject to |v| = 1 gives S v = lambda v),
   SVM and regularization as constrained problems (Module 48), KKT
   conditions (Appendix D).

GRADIENT-DESCENT MICRO EXAMPLE: f(x, y) = x^2 + 3 y^2, start (2, 1),
learning rate eta = 0.1: grad f = (2x, 6y) = (4, 6); new point
(2 - 0.4, 1 - 0.6) = (1.6, 0.4); f falls from 7 to 2.56 + 0.48 = 3.04.

blocks.title: DOUBLE INTEGRAL AND ITERATED INTEGRALS
blocks.formulaBody:
Double integral: int int_R f(x, y) dA = lim sum f(x_i*, y_j*) Delta A
     Over a rectangle [a, b] x [c, d] (Fubini):
        int int f dA = int[a..b] ( int[c..d] f(x, y) dy ) dx
                     = int[c..d] ( int[a..b] f(x, y) dx ) dy.
     Type I region (between curves of x): R = {a <= x <= b, g1(x) <= y <= g2(x)}:
        int int_R f dA = int[a..b] int[g1(x)..g2(x)] f(x, y) dy dx.
     Type II region: R = {c <= y <= d, h1(y) <= x <= h2(y)}:
        int int_R f dA = int[c..d] int[h1(y)..h2(y)] f(x, y) dx dy.
     AREA of R = int int_R 1 dA.
     VOLUME under z = f(x, y) >= 0 above R = int int_R f dA.

parts.C: SYMBOLS: dA = dx dy an infinitesimal area element; R the region.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: slice the region into tiny rectangles of area Delta A; the volume
   over each is height f times area; sum and take the limit. In practice
   compute two single integrals: inner first (treating the outer variable
   as a constant), then outer.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: f continuous on R (Fubini: integrable and bounded suffices);
   the limits of the INNER integral may depend on the OUTER variable only,
   never on itself; the OUTER limits must be constants. You may swap the
   order if you also redraw the limits.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple (rectangle): int[0..1] int[0..2] (x + y) dy dx.
        Inner: [x y + y^2/2] from y = 0 to 2 = 2x + 2.
        Outer: int[0..1] (2x + 2) dx = [x^2 + 2x] = 3.
   Moderate (triangle 0 <= y <= x <= 1): int[0..1] int[0..x] x y dy dx.
        Inner: x [y^2/2] from 0 to x = x^3/2.
        Outer: int[0..1] x^3/2 dx = 1/8.
        Swapping order: int[0..1] int[y..1] x y dx dy = int y (1 - y^2)/2 dy
        = (1/2)(1/2 - 1/4) = 1/8. Same.
   Moderate 2 (probability): joint density f(x, y) = 2 on the triangle
        0 <= y <= x <= 1 (area 1/2, so density 2 integrates to 1).
        P(X <= 1/2) = int[0..1/2] int[0..x] 2 dy dx = int[0..1/2] 2x dx
        = 1/4.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: the average value of f over R is (1/Area) int int_R f dA.
   Marginal density of X from a joint density: f_X(x) = int f(x, y) dy
   (Module 35).

sections.title: POLAR, CYLINDRICAL AND SPHERICAL COORDINATES

blocks.title: COORDINATE SYSTEMS AND AREA/VOLUME ELEMENTS
blocks.formulaBody:
POLAR (2D): x = r cos(theta), y = r sin(theta), r >= 0, 0 <= theta < 2 pi.
        r^2 = x^2 + y^2.   dA = r dr d(theta).
   CYLINDRICAL (3D): x = r cos(theta), y = r sin(theta), z = z.
        dV = r dz dr d(theta).
   SPHERICAL (3D): x = rho sin(phi) cos(theta), y = rho sin(phi) sin(theta),
        z = rho cos(phi); rho >= 0 (distance from the origin),
        0 <= phi <= pi (angle from the +z axis), 0 <= theta < 2 pi.
        rho^2 = x^2 + y^2 + z^2.   dV = rho^2 sin(phi) d(rho) d(phi) d(theta).

parts.B:
POLAR (2D): x = r cos(theta), y = r sin(theta), r >= 0, 0 <= theta < 2 pi.
        r^2 = x^2 + y^2.   dA = r dr d(theta).
   CYLINDRICAL (3D): x = r cos(theta), y = r sin(theta), z = z.
        dV = r dz dr d(theta).
   SPHERICAL (3D): x = rho sin(phi) cos(theta), y = rho sin(phi) sin(theta),
        z = rho cos(phi); rho >= 0 (distance from the origin),
        0 <= phi <= pi (angle from the +z axis), 0 <= theta < 2 pi.
        rho^2 = x^2 + y^2 + z^2.   dV = rho^2 sin(phi) d(rho) d(phi) d(theta).
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: r radial distance from the z-axis (or origin in 2D); theta
   azimuth angle in the xy-plane; phi polar angle from the z-axis; rho
   distance from the origin. CONVENTION NOTE: physics-style (phi from
   the z-axis, theta azimuth) as above; mathematics texts sometimes swap
   the symbols theta and phi. State the convention before using.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: use these when the region or integrand has circular or
   spherical symmetry. The extra factors r and rho^2 sin(phi) account for how
   a small coordinate "box" stretches (area of a polar patch is
   r dr d(theta), not dr d(theta)).
parts.E: CONDITIONS: set the angular limits to cover the region exactly once.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: area of a disc of radius R: int[0..2pi] int[0..R] r dr d(theta)
        = 2 pi R^2/2 = pi R^2.
   Moderate 1 (volume under a paraboloid): region under z = 4 - x^2 - y^2
        above z = 0 (so r <= 2): int[0..2pi] int[0..2] (4 - r^2) r dr d(theta)
        = 2 pi [2 r^2 - r^4/4] from 0 to 2 = 2 pi (8 - 4) = 8 pi.
   Moderate 2 (the Gaussian integral): I(R) = int int_(x^2+y^2 <= R^2)
        e^(-(x^2 + y^2)) dA = int[0..2pi] int[0..R] e^(-r^2) r dr d(theta)
        = 2 pi * (1 - e^(-R^2))/2 = pi (1 - e^(-R^2)).
        As R -> inf this tends to pi, and since the integral over the
        whole plane equals (int e^(-x^2) dx)^2, we get
        int[-inf..inf] e^(-x^2) dx = sqrt(pi). (Hence int e^(-x^2/2) dx
        = sqrt(2 pi), as used in Module 4 and the normal density.)
   Moderate 3 (sphere): volume of a ball of radius R:
        int[0..2pi] int[0..pi] int[0..R] rho^2 sin(phi) d(rho) d(phi) d(theta)
        = 2 pi * 2 * R^3/3 = (4/3) pi R^3.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: r dr d(theta) is the true area of a small polar
   patch; spherical volume elements grow like rho^2.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: forgetting the Jacobian factor r or rho^2 sin(phi); mixing the
   roles of theta and phi; wrong limits (phi up to pi, not 2 pi).
parts.J: RELATED: Jacobian (F13.3); the Gaussian integral (Module 13.3).

        = 2 pi [2 r^2 - r^4/4] from 0 to 2 = 2 pi (8 - 4) = 8 pi.
   Moderate 2 (the Gaussian integral): I(R) = int int_(x^2+y^2 <= R^2)
        e^(-(x^2 + y^2)) dA = int[0..2pi] int[0..R] e^(-r^2) r dr d(theta)
        = 2 pi * (1 - e^(-R^2))/2 = pi (1 - e^(-R^2)).
        As R -> inf this tends to pi, and since the integral over the
        whole plane equals (int e^(-x^2) dx)^2, we get
        int[-inf..inf] e^(-x^2) dx = sqrt(pi). (Hence int e^(-x^2/2) dx
        = sqrt(2 pi), as used in Module 4 and the normal density.)
   Moderate 3 (sphere): volume of a ball of radius R:
        int[0..2pi] int[0..pi] int[0..R] rho^2 sin(phi) d(rho) d(phi) d(theta)
        = 2 pi * 2 * R^3/3 = (4/3) pi R^3.
H. INTERPRETATION: r dr d(theta) is the true area of a small polar
   patch; spherical volume elements grow like rho^2.
I. MISTAKES: forgetting the Jacobian factor r or rho^2 sin(phi); mixing the
   roles of theta and phi; wrong limits (phi up to pi, not 2 pi).
J. RELATED: Jacobian (F13.3); the Gaussian integral (Module 13.3).

sections.title: CHANGE OF VARIABLES AND THE JACOBIAN (INTRODUCTORY)

blocks.title: CHANGE OF VARIABLES
blocks.formulaBody:
for a transformation x = x(u, v), y = y(u, v) mapping a region S
   in the (u, v)-plane one-to-one onto R in the (x, y)-plane:
        int int_R f(x, y) dx dy = int int_S f( x(u,v), y(u,v) ) |J| du dv
        J = det [ x_u  x_v ; y_u  y_v ] = x_u y_v - x_v y_u.
   (In n dimensions, J = det of the matrix of partial derivatives.)

parts.A: NAME: Change of variables formula; Jacobian determinant.
parts.B:
FORMULA: for a transformation x = x(u, v), y = y(u, v) mapping a region S
   in the (u, v)-plane one-to-one onto R in the (x, y)-plane:
        int int_R f(x, y) dx dy = int int_S f( x(u,v), y(u,v) ) |J| du dv
        J = det [ x_u  x_v ; y_u  y_v ] = x_u y_v - x_v y_u.
   (In n dimensions, J = det of the matrix of partial derivatives.)
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: J (Jacobian determinant): the local area-scaling factor of the
   map (u, v) -> (x, y); |J| its absolute value.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: a tiny rectangle du x dv maps to a tiny parallelogram with area
   |J| du dv. J generalizes the factor 1/g'(x) in single-variable
   u-substitution (F4.5).
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: the map must be one-to-one (invertible) with continuous
   partial derivatives and J != 0.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Polar: x = r cos t, y = r sin t: J = det [cos t, -r sin t ; sin t,
        r cos t] = r cos^2 t + r sin^2 t = r. So dx dy = r dr dt. OK.
   Linear map: x = 2u + v, y = u - v: J = det [2 1 ; 1 -1] = -3; |J| = 3;
        areas are multiplied by 3 (and orientation reversed).
   Moderate (ellipse area): x = a u, y = b v maps the unit disc onto
        x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 <= 1; |J| = a b; area = a b * pi.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: transformation of random variables: if Y = g(X) (n
   dimensions), f_Y(y) = f_X(g^(-1)(y)) |det J_(g^(-1))(y)|; normalizing
   flows in ML use exactly this formula.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: forgetting the absolute value; using J of the inverse map
   inverted (use the right direction); not checking one-to-one.
parts.J: RELATED: determinant as volume scaling (F6.9).

sections.title: PARAMETRIC EQUATIONS

blocks.rawText:
BASIC IDEA: Instead of y = f(x), describe a curve by giving x and y as
functions of a PARAMETER t (often time): x = x(t), y = y(t). As t
increases, the point (x(t), y(t)) traces the curve. Advantages: curves
that fail the vertical-line test (circles), direction of travel, speed.

COMMON PARAMETRIZATIONS
   Line:        (x0 + t d1, y0 + t d2)
   Circle:      (R cos t, R sin t),  0 <= t < 2 pi   (anticlockwise)
   Ellipse:     (a cos t, b sin t)
   Parabola:    (t, t^2)  or (2 t, t^2)
   Cycloid:     (t - sin t, 1 - cos t)
   Projectile:  (v0 cos(alpha) t, h + v0 sin(alpha) t - g t^2/2)
ELIMINATING THE PARAMETER: solve one equation for t and substitute, or use
identities (cos^2 t + sin^2 t = 1). Example: x = 3 cos t, y = 2 sin t gives
(x/3)^2 + (y/2)^2 = 1: an ellipse.
!! NOTE !! The same curve has many parametrizations (e.g. (cos 2t, sin 2t)
traces the unit circle twice as fast).

blocks.title: SLOPE OF A PARAMETRIC CURVE
blocks.formulaBody:
dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt)   (dx/dt != 0).
   Second derivative: d^2y/dx^2 = d/dt(dy/dx) / (dx/dt).

parts.B:
dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt)   (dx/dt != 0).
   Second derivative: d^2y/dx^2 = d/dt(dy/dx) / (dx/dt).
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: x(t), y(t) the coordinate functions; dx/dt, dy/dt their
   derivatives; dy/dx the slope of the curve.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the chain rule dy/dt = (dy/dx)(dx/dt) solved for dy/dx; the
   slope is the ratio of vertical to horizontal speed.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: dx/dt != 0 (dx/dt = 0 with dy/dt != 0 gives a vertical
   tangent); x(t) and y(t) differentiable.
parts.G:
EXAMPLE: x = t^2, y = t^3: dy/dx = 3t^2/(2t) = 3t/2 (t != 0). At t = 2:
   point (4, 8), slope 3.
parts.H: INTERPRETATION: the direction of travel of a trajectory.
parts.I:
MISTAKE: differentiating dy/dx with respect to x as if it were t:
   the second derivative needs the extra division by dx/dt.
parts.J:
RELATED: chain rule (F3.7), implicit differentiation (F3.10),
   velocity vector (F14.2).

sections.title: VECTOR-VALUED FUNCTIONS; POSITION, VELOCITY, ACCELERATION

blocks.title: VECTOR-VALUED FUNCTIONS OF ONE VARIABLE
blocks.formulaBody:
r(t) = ( x(t), y(t), z(t) )   (position vector)
   v(t) = r'(t) = ( x'(t), y'(t), z'(t) )   velocity (tangent to the curve)
   speed = |v(t)| = sqrt( x'^2 + y'^2 + z'^2 )
   a(t) = r''(t)   acceleration
   Unit tangent T(t) = r'(t)/|r'(t)|  (needs r' != 0).

parts.B:
r(t) = ( x(t), y(t), z(t) )   (position vector)
   v(t) = r'(t) = ( x'(t), y'(t), z'(t) )   velocity (tangent to the curve)
   speed = |v(t)| = sqrt( x'^2 + y'^2 + z'^2 )
   a(t) = r''(t)   acceleration
   Unit tangent T(t) = r'(t)/|r'(t)|  (needs r' != 0).
parts.C: SYMBOLS: derivatives are taken component by component with respect to t.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: velocity points along the direction of motion; its length is the
   speed; acceleration measures change of velocity (direction OR speed).
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: components differentiable; the unit tangent requires
   r'(t) != 0.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: r(t) = (3t, 4t): v = (3, 4), speed 5 constant, a = 0
        (straight-line, constant velocity).
   Moderate: circular motion r(t) = (R cos(w t), R sin(w t)):
        v = (-R w sin(wt), R w cos(wt)); speed = R w (constant);
        a = (-R w^2 cos(wt), -R w^2 sin(wt)) = -w^2 r(t): acceleration points
        toward the center with magnitude R w^2 (centripetal acceleration),
        even though the SPEED is constant. v . r = 0 (velocity is
        perpendicular to the position vector).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: r' is the instantaneous direction and speed of
   motion; r'' tells how the motion bends or accelerates.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: confusing speed (a scalar |v|) and velocity (a vector);
   assuming zero acceleration at constant speed (direction changes).
parts.J:
RELATED: arc length (F14.3), parametrizations (section 14.1),
   gradient flow (F16.5).

sections.title: ARC LENGTH; DISTANCE FROM A POINT TO THE ORIGIN

blocks.title: ARC LENGTH
blocks.formulaBody:
L = int[a..b] |r'(t)| dt = int[a..b] sqrt( x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2 + z'(t)^2 ) dt
     For a graph y = f(x):  L = int[a..b] sqrt( 1 + (f'(x))^2 ) dx.
     Arc-length function s(t) = int[a..t] |r'(u)| du; ds/dt = |r'(t)|.

parts.A: NAME: Arc length of a parametric curve.
parts.B:
FORMULAS
     L = int[a..b] |r'(t)| dt = int[a..b] sqrt( x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2 + z'(t)^2 ) dt
     For a graph y = f(x):  L = int[a..b] sqrt( 1 + (f'(x))^2 ) dx.
     Arc-length function s(t) = int[a..t] |r'(u)| du; ds/dt = |r'(t)|.
parts.C: SYMBOLS: |r'(t)| speed; [a, b] the parameter interval.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: "distance = integral of speed". Chop the curve into tiny straight
   segments of length sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2) = |r'| dt and add them up.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: r' continuous; the curve should be traced ONCE over [a, b]
   (otherwise the formula gives total distance traveled, which
   counts repeats).
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: circle of radius R over 0 <= t <= 2 pi: speed R: L = 2 pi R.
   Moderate (helix): r(t) = (cos t, sin t, t), 0 <= t <= 2 pi:
        r' = (-sin t, cos t, 1), speed = sqrt(sin^2 t + cos^2 t + 1)
        = sqrt(2); L = 2 pi sqrt(2) = 8.886.
        (General helix (a cos t, a sin t, b t): speed sqrt(a^2 + b^2);
        one turn has length 2 pi sqrt(a^2 + b^2).)
   Moderate 2 (graph): y = x^(3/2) on [0, 1]: f' = (3/2) x^(1/2),
        1 + f'^2 = 1 + (9/4) x.
        L = int[0..1] sqrt(1 + 9x/4) dx = (8/27) [ (1 + 9x/4)^(3/2) ] from 0
        to 1 = (8/27)( (13/4)^(3/2) - 1 ) = (8/27)(5.8590 - 1) = 1.4397.
        (Slightly longer than the chord from (0,0) to (1,1), of length
        1.4142, as expected.)
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: path length of an optimization trajectory, total
   variation of a time series, length of a decision boundary.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: forgetting the square root; integrating a velocity vector
   instead of its magnitude; including a repeated traversal.
parts.J: RELATED: speed (F14.2); graph length from the parametrization x = t.

blocks.formulaBody:
d(t) = |r(t)| = sqrt( x(t)^2 + y(t)^2 + z(t)^2 ).
   To find the CLOSEST point of a curve to the origin, minimize d(t)^2
   (same minimizer, no square root): solve d/dt ( |r(t)|^2 ) = 2 r . r' = 0.

        1.4142, as expected.)

sections.title: CURVES IN 3D; CIRCULAR AND HELICAL MOTION

blocks.rawText:
SUMMARY
   Circle in the xy-plane: (R cos t, R sin t, 0).
   Circle in a tilted plane: r(t) = c + R cos(t) u + R sin(t) w with u, w
     orthonormal vectors in the plane.

     ("pitch"); constant speed sqrt(a^2 + b^2); acceleration magnitude
     a (angular rate 1).

     (an ellipse): parametrize (cos t, sin t, cos t + sin t).

polynomials; time series as curves in feature space; embeddings
trajectories; "path length" as a smoothness measure.

sections.title: WHAT DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS REPRESENT

blocks.rawText:
BASIC IDEA (plain English)
An ordinary algebra equation asks "which NUMBER satisfies this?". A
differential equation asks "which FUNCTION satisfies this?", where the
equation links the function to its own rates of change. Nature usually
tells us rules about change, not about the quantity itself:
  - "A population grows at a rate proportional to its size."
  - "A hot object cools at a rate proportional to the temperature gap."
  - "Parameters move in the direction that decreases the loss."
Solving the differential equation turns the rule about change into the
actual curve.

blocks.title: GENERAL FORM
blocks.formulaBody:
An ODE for an unknown function y(t) (or y(x)):
        F( t, y, y', y'', ..., y^(n) ) = 0.
   Typical first-order form: y' = f(t, y)  (dy/dt = f(t, y)).

parts.B:
An ODE for an unknown function y(t) (or y(x)):
        F( t, y, y', y'', ..., y^(n) ) = 0.
   Typical first-order form: y' = f(t, y)  (dy/dt = f(t, y)).
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: t (or x) the independent variable; y the unknown function;
   y', y'' its derivatives; n the highest derivative present.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: f(t, y) gives the slope of the solution curve at each point
   (t, y): a "direction field". A solution is a curve that follows these
   slopes everywhere.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES OF MODELS
   Exponential growth/decay:   dy/dt = k y
   Newton's cooling:           dT/dt = -k (T - T_env)
   Logistic growth:            dy/dt = r y (1 - y/K)
   Spring (2nd order):         m y'' + c y' + k y = 0
   Gradient flow (ML):         d(theta)/dt = - grad L(theta)
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: ODEs encode rules about change; the solution
   reconstructs the quantity from those rules.
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: confusing ODEs with PDEs; forgetting the arbitrary
   constants of the general solution; not checking a solution by
   substitution.
parts.J:
RELATED: separable equations (F16.1), linear first-order equations
   (F16.2), gradient flow (F16.5).

sections.title: ORDINARY vs PARTIAL; ORDER AND DEGREE

blocks.rawText:
ODE: unknown function of ONE independent variable, ordinary derivatives.
PDE: unknown function of SEVERAL variables, partial derivatives.
   Example PDE (heat equation): PARTIAL u/PARTIAL t = alpha PARTIAL^2 u/
   PARTIAL x^2.  PDEs are outside this syllabus beyond this distinction.

ORDER: the highest derivative that appears.
   y' + 3y = 0 : order 1.   y'' + 3 y' + 2 y = 0 : order 2.
   (y''')^2 + y = x : order 3.
DEGREE [SYLLABUS NOTE 2]: the power of the highest-order derivative once the
   equation is written as a polynomial in the derivatives. Convention
   used here: degree is only defined if the equation is polynomial in
   its derivatives.
   (y')^3 + y = x : order 1, degree 3.
   y'' + (y')^4 = 0 : order 2, degree 1 (the highest derivative y'' has
   power 1).
   sin(y') + y = 0 : order 1, degree NOT defined (not polynomial in y').
   Many modern textbooks use "linear / nonlinear" instead of degree.

LINEAR vs NONLINEAR: an ODE is LINEAR if y and its derivatives appear only
   to the first power and are not multiplied together or inside
   functions:  a_n(t) y^(n) + ... + a_1(t) y' + a_0(t) y = g(t).
   Linear: y' + 2y = e^t.   Nonlinear: y' = y^2, y y' = t, y'' + sin(y) = 0.
   Linear homogeneous: g(t) = 0 (then sums and multiples of solutions are
   also solutions: the SUPERPOSITION principle).
AUTONOMOUS: the right-hand side does not contain t explicitly: y' = f(y).

sections.title: GENERAL AND PARTICULAR SOLUTIONS; INITIAL VALUE PROBLEMS

blocks.rawText:
GENERAL SOLUTION: the family of ALL solutions; an n-th order ODE has a
   general solution with n arbitrary constants.
   Example: y' = 2y has general solution y = C e^(2t). (Check: y' = 2 C
   e^(2t) = 2y.)
PARTICULAR SOLUTION: one member of the family, found by fixing the
   constants.
INITIAL VALUE PROBLEM (IVP): ODE plus n initial conditions at one point
   (for first order: y(t0) = y0).
   Example: y' = 2y, y(0) = 3: C e^0 = 3 -> C = 3: y = 3 e^(2t).
SINGULAR SOLUTION: an extra solution not obtainable from the general
   family (rare, appears in nonlinear equations).
HOW TO CHECK A CLAIMED SOLUTION: substitute y and its derivatives into
   the ODE; check that both sides agree for all t, then check the
   initial condition.
   Example: Is y = t^2 + 1/t a solution of t y' - 2 y = -3/t ... ?
   y' = 2t - 1/t^2: t y' = 2 t^2 - 1/t. 2 y = 2 t^2 + 2/t.
   t y' - 2 y = -1/t - 2/t = -3/t. Yes.
COMMON MISTAKES: forgetting the constant; imposing the initial
   condition BEFORE the constant of integration has been introduced
   correctly (apply it to the general solution); losing solutions by
   dividing by an expression that may be zero.

sections.title: EXISTENCE AND UNIQUENESS OF SOLUTIONS

blocks.title: PICARD-LINDELOF (EXISTENCE AND UNIQUENESS) THEOREM
blocks.formulaBody:
consider y' = f(t, y), y(t0) = y0. If f and its partial
   derivative f_y = PARTIAL f/PARTIAL y are continuous in a rectangle
   around (t0, y0), then there exists a solution on some (possibly
   small) interval around t0, and that solution is UNIQUE there.

parts.A: NAME: Existence and uniqueness theorem for first-order IVPs.
parts.B:
STATEMENT: consider y' = f(t, y), y(t0) = y0. If f and its partial
   derivative f_y = PARTIAL f/PARTIAL y are continuous in a rectangle
   around (t0, y0), then there exists a solution on some (possibly
   small) interval around t0, and that solution is UNIQUE there.
parts.C: SYMBOLS: f_y the partial derivative with respect to y (Module 12).
parts.D:
CONCEPT: continuity of f gives existence (a solution can follow the
   slope field); the smoothness of f in y prevents two different
   solutions from branching out of the same point.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: the guarantee is LOCAL (solutions may blow up in finite
   time) and sufficient, not necessary. When f_y fails to be continuous,
   uniqueness may fail.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Existence + uniqueness: y' = y^2, y(0) = 1: f = y^2, f_y = 2y
        continuous everywhere: unique solution y = 1/(1 - t) which blows
        up at t = 1 (a finite-time "explosion": solution exists only on
        t < 1).
   Uniqueness FAILS: y' = 3 y^(2/3), y(0) = 0. f_y = 2 y^(-1/3) is not
        continuous at y = 0. Both y(t) = 0 and y(t) = t^3 solve it
        (check: (t^3)' = 3 t^2 = 3 (t^3)^(2/3) = 3 t^2).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: a well-posed model should have exactly one trajectory
   for each initial state; non-uniqueness signals a modeling problem.
parts.I:
MISTAKE: assuming a solution exists for all t because the right-hand
   side looks harmless.
parts.J:
RELATED: Lipschitz continuity (a stronger form of the condition on
   f_y); numerical solution (F16.5).

sections.title: SEPARABLE DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS

blocks.title: SEPARATION OF VARIABLES
blocks.formulaBody:
an ODE of the form  dy/dx = g(x) h(y)  is solved by
        (1/h(y)) dy = g(x) dx   =>   int dy/h(y) = int g(x) dx + C.

parts.B:
FORMULA: an ODE of the form  dy/dx = g(x) h(y)  is solved by
        (1/h(y)) dy = g(x) dx   =>   int dy/h(y) = int g(x) dx + C.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: g(x) depends only on x; h(y) only on y; C a single constant of
   integration.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: collect all y on one side and all x on the other, then
   integrate both sides. The key: the rate of change factorizes into a
   "time part" and a "state part".
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: dividing by h(y) is allowed only where h(y) != 0.
   Constants y* with h(y*) = 0 are EQUILIBRIUM solutions and must be
   checked separately (they may be lost by the division).
parts.F:
IDEA: dy/dx = g h is "dy/h = g dx" treating dy/dx as a ratio of
   differentials; rigorously it follows from the chain rule and
   substitution (F4.5).
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: dy/dx = x y, y(0) = 2.
        dy/y = x dx -> ln|y| = x^2/2 + C -> y = A e^(x^2/2) (A = +/- e^C).
        y(0) = 2 -> A = 2: y = 2 e^(x^2/2).
        Lost solution: y = 0 (equilibrium), covered by A = 0.
   Moderate (logistic, the sigmoid appears!): dy/dt = y (1 - y), y(0) = 1/2.
        dy / (y (1 - y)) = dt. Partial fractions:
        1/(y(1 - y)) = 1/y + 1/(1 - y).
        ln|y| - ln|1 - y| = t + C -> y/(1 - y) = A e^t.
        Solve: y = A e^t / (1 + A e^t). y(0) = 1/2 -> A/(1 + A) = 1/2 ->
        A = 1: y = e^t/(1 + e^t) = 1/(1 + e^(-t)): the sigmoid function.
        Equilibria: y = 0 and y = 1 (checked separately).
   Moderate 2: dy/dx = (1 + y^2) (variables separated):
        arctan y = x + C -> y = tan(x + C): blows up at finite x.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: the logistic ODE explains the S-shaped growth curve:
   exponential-like growth at first, saturating at the carrying
   capacity (K = 1 here). The sigmoid in logistic regression is this
   curve.
parts.J:
RELATED: integrating factors (F16.2), equilibria (F16.4), integration
   techniques (Module 4).

blocks.rawText:
F16.1  SEPARATION OF VARIABLES
A. NAME: Separable ODE method.
B. FORMULA: an ODE of the form  dy/dx = g(x) h(y)  is solved by
        (1/h(y)) dy = g(x) dx   =>   int dy/h(y) = int g(x) dx + C.
C. SYMBOLS: g(x) depends only on x; h(y) only on y; C a single constant of
   integration.
D. CONCEPT: collect all y on one side and all x on the other, then
   integrate both sides. The key: the rate of change factorizes into a
   "time part" and a "state part".
E. CONDITIONS: dividing by h(y) is allowed only where h(y) != 0.
   Constants y* with h(y*) = 0 are EQUILIBRIUM solutions and must be
   checked separately (they may be lost by the division).
F. IDEA: dy/dx = g h is "dy/h = g dx" treating dy/dx as a ratio of
   differentials; rigorously it follows from the chain rule and
   substitution (F4.5).
G. EXAMPLES
   Simple: dy/dx = x y, y(0) = 2.
        dy/y = x dx -> ln|y| = x^2/2 + C -> y = A e^(x^2/2) (A = +/- e^C).
        y(0) = 2 -> A = 2: y = 2 e^(x^2/2).
        Lost solution: y = 0 (equilibrium), covered by A = 0.
   Moderate (logistic, the sigmoid appears!): dy/dt = y (1 - y), y(0) = 1/2.
        dy / (y (1 - y)) = dt. Partial fractions:
        1/(y(1 - y)) = 1/y + 1/(1 - y).
        ln|y| - ln|1 - y| = t + C -> y/(1 - y) = A e^t.
        Solve: y = A e^t / (1 + A e^t). y(0) = 1/2 -> A/(1 + A) = 1/2 ->
        A = 1: y = e^t/(1 + e^t) = 1/(1 + e^(-t)): the sigmoid function.
        Equilibria: y = 0 and y = 1 (checked separately).
   Moderate 2: dy/dx = (1 + y^2) (variables separated):
        arctan y = x + C -> y = tan(x + C): blows up at finite x.
H. INTERPRETATION: the logistic ODE explains the S-shaped growth curve:
   exponential-like growth at first, saturating at the carrying
   capacity (K = 1 here). The sigmoid in logistic regression is this
   curve.
I. MISTAKES: forgetting the constant; losing equilibrium solutions;
   dropping absolute values inside logs without justification;
   attempting to separate an equation that does not factorize
   (e.g. dy/dx = x + y is NOT separable; it is linear).
J. RELATED: integrating factors (F16.2), equilibria (F16.4), integration
   techniques (Module 4).

sections.title: LINEAR FIRST-ORDER EQUATIONS AND INTEGRATING FACTORS

blocks.title: INTEGRATING FACTOR METHOD
blocks.formulaBody:
Standard form:  y' + P(x) y = Q(x).
     Integrating factor:  mu(x) = exp( int P(x) dx ).
     Then (mu y)' = mu Q, so
        y = (1/mu(x)) ( int mu(x) Q(x) dx + C ).

parts.A: NAME: Integrating factor for first-order linear ODEs.
parts.B:
FORMULA
     Standard form:  y' + P(x) y = Q(x).
     Integrating factor:  mu(x) = exp( int P(x) dx ).
     Then (mu y)' = mu Q, so
        y = (1/mu(x)) ( int mu(x) Q(x) dx + C ).
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: P, Q given functions; mu the integrating factor (any
   antiderivative of P may be used: the constant cancels).
parts.D:
CONCEPT: multiplying by mu converts the left-hand side into a perfect
   derivative by the product rule: (mu y)' = mu y' + mu' y, and mu' =
   P mu by construction. Then just integrate.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: the equation must be LINEAR in y and put into STANDARD FORM
   (coefficient of y' equal to 1) before reading off P(x).
parts.F:
DERIVATION: demand mu y' + mu P y = (mu y)' = mu y' + mu' y, so
   mu' = P mu, i.e. d(ln mu)/dx = P, giving mu = exp(int P dx).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: the solution splits into a TRANSIENT part (C e^(-2x),
   which decays) and a part that follows the forcing term (e^(-x)). This
   "homogeneous + particular" structure mirrors F7.3 in linear algebra.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: not dividing by the coefficient of y' first (reading P from
   x y' + 2y as 2); forgetting to multiply the RIGHT side by mu; leaving
   out the 1/mu when solving for y; forgetting C.
parts.J:
RELATED: separable method (for y' + P y = 0 the two methods agree:
   y = C exp(-int P)).

blocks.rawText:
F16.2  INTEGRATING FACTOR METHOD
A. NAME: Integrating factor for first-order linear ODEs.
B. FORMULA
     Standard form:  y' + P(x) y = Q(x).
     Integrating factor:  mu(x) = exp( int P(x) dx ).
     Then (mu y)' = mu Q, so
        y = (1/mu(x)) ( int mu(x) Q(x) dx + C ).
C. SYMBOLS: P, Q given functions; mu the integrating factor (any
   antiderivative of P may be used: the constant cancels).
D. CONCEPT: multiplying by mu converts the left-hand side into a perfect
   derivative by the product rule: (mu y)' = mu y' + mu' y, and mu' =
   P mu by construction. Then just integrate.
E. CONDITIONS: the equation must be LINEAR in y and put into STANDARD FORM
   (coefficient of y' equal to 1) before reading off P(x).
F. DERIVATION: demand mu y' + mu P y = (mu y)' = mu y' + mu' y, so
   mu' = P mu, i.e. d(ln mu)/dx = P, giving mu = exp(int P dx).
G. EXAMPLES
   Simple: y' + 2y = e^(-x), y(0) = 3. P = 2, mu = e^(2x).
        (e^(2x) y)' = e^(2x) e^(-x) = e^x -> e^(2x) y = e^x + C
        -> y = e^(-x) + C e^(-2x). y(0) = 1 + C = 3 -> C = 2:
        y = e^(-x) + 2 e^(-2x).
        Check: y' + 2y = -e^(-x) - 4 e^(-2x) + 2 e^(-x) + 4 e^(-2x) = e^(-x). OK.
   Moderate: x y' + 2 y = x^2, x > 0, y(1) = 2.
        Standard form: y' + (2/x) y = x. P = 2/x; mu = exp(2 ln x) = x^2.
        (x^2 y)' = x^3 -> x^2 y = x^4/4 + C -> y = x^2/4 + C/x^2.
        y(1) = 1/4 + C = 2 -> C = 7/4: y = x^2/4 + 7/(4 x^2).
        Check: y' = x/2 - 7/(2 x^3). x y' = x^2/2 - 7/(2 x^2);
        2 y = x^2/2 + 7/(2 x^2); sum = x^2. OK.
H. INTERPRETATION: the solution splits into a TRANSIENT part (C e^(-2x),
   which decays) and a part that follows the forcing term (e^(-x)). This
   "homogeneous + particular" structure mirrors F7.3 in linear algebra.
I. MISTAKES: not dividing by the coefficient of y' first (reading P from
   x y' + 2y as 2); forgetting to multiply the RIGHT side by mu; leaving
   out the 1/mu when solving for y; forgetting C.
J. RELATED: separable method (for y' + P y = 0 the two methods agree:
   y = C exp(-int P)).

sections.title: INITIAL CONDITIONS; EXPONENTIAL GROWTH AND DECAY

blocks.title: EXPONENTIAL GROWTH/DECAY MODEL
blocks.formulaBody:
dy/dt = k y  with y(0) = y0   =>   y(t) = y0 e^(k t).
     k > 0: growth;  k < 0: decay.
     Doubling time = ln 2 / k;  half-life = ln 2 / |k|.
     Newton's cooling: dT/dt = -k (T - T_env)  =>
        T(t) = T_env + (T0 - T_env) e^(-k t).
     Linear with constant term: dy/dt = a y + b (a != 0) =>
        y(t) = -b/a + ( y0 + b/a ) e^(a t).

parts.B:
FORMULA
     dy/dt = k y  with y(0) = y0   =>   y(t) = y0 e^(k t).
     k > 0: growth;  k < 0: decay.
     Doubling time = ln 2 / k;  half-life = ln 2 / |k|.
     Newton's cooling: dT/dt = -k (T - T_env)  =>
        T(t) = T_env + (T0 - T_env) e^(-k t).
     Linear with constant term: dy/dt = a y + b (a != 0) =>
        y(t) = -b/a + ( y0 + b/a ) e^(a t).
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: k constant relative rate of change (per unit time); y0 initial
   value; T_env the surrounding temperature.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the rate of change is proportional to the current amount, so the
   relative change per unit time is constant.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: k constant; resources unlimited for growth (otherwise
   logistic). Cooling law assumes uniform temperature of the object.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple (decay): 100 g with half-life 5 years: k = -ln 2/5 = -0.1386;
        after 12 years: y = 100 e^(-0.1386 * 12) = 100 * 2^(-12/5)
        = 100 * 0.18946 = 18.95 g.
   Moderate (cooling): coffee at 90 C in a 20 C room reaches 60 C after
        10 minutes. 60 = 20 + 70 e^(-10k) -> e^(-10k) = 40/70 = 4/7 ->
        k = ln(7/4)/10 = 0.05596 per minute.
        At 20 minutes: T = 20 + 70 (4/7)^2 = 20 + 70 * 16/49 = 42.86 C.
        Long-term: T -> 20 C.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: k is a rate constant; 1/|k| is the "time constant" (the
   time for a 63% change toward equilibrium).
parts.I:
MISTAKES: using years for k and months for t; using the half-life as k;
   forgetting that cooling approaches T_env, not zero.
parts.J:
RELATED: exponential moving averages and learning-rate decay
   (eta_t = eta_0 e^(-k t)) are the discrete analogs.

sections.title: EQUILIBRIUM SOLUTIONS AND LONG-TERM BEHAVIOR

blocks.title: EQUILIBRIA OF AUTONOMOUS EQUATIONS y' = f(y)
blocks.formulaBody:
EQUILIBRIUM (constant) solution y = y*: f(y*) = 0.
   STABILITY (linearization): if f'(y*) < 0 the equilibrium is STABLE
   (a sink: nearby solutions approach it); if f'(y*) > 0 it is UNSTABLE
   (a source: solutions move away). If f'(y*) = 0: inconclusive; use the
   sign of f around y*.
   Phase-line rule: y increases where f(y) > 0 and decreases where f(y) < 0.

parts.B:
EQUILIBRIUM (constant) solution y = y*: f(y*) = 0.
   STABILITY (linearization): if f'(y*) < 0 the equilibrium is STABLE
   (a sink: nearby solutions approach it); if f'(y*) > 0 it is UNSTABLE
   (a source: solutions move away). If f'(y*) = 0: inconclusive; use the
   sign of f around y*.
   Phase-line rule: y increases where f(y) > 0 and decreases where f(y) < 0.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: y* an equilibrium (f(y*) = 0); f'(y*) the slope of f there
   (stability indicator).
parts.D:
CONCEPT: solutions of y' = f(y) never cross (uniqueness), and being
   monotone they either settle to an equilibrium or run off to infinity.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: the equation is autonomous (no explicit t); linearization
   is conclusive when f'(y*) != 0.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Linear: y' = -2 (y - 3): equilibrium y* = 3; f' = -2 < 0: stable.
        Solution y = 3 + (y0 - 3) e^(-2t) -> 3 as t -> inf for every y0.
   Logistic: y' = r y (1 - y/K): f(y) = r y (1 - y/K); equilibria 0 and K.
        f'(y) = r (1 - 2y/K): f'(0) = r > 0: UNSTABLE; f'(K) = -r < 0:
        STABLE. Any positive initial population tends to K.
   Moderate: y' = y^2 - 4 = (y - 2)(y + 2): equilibria -2, 2.
        f' = 2y: f'(-2) = -4 < 0 stable; f'(2) = 4 > 0 unstable.
        y(0) = 0 (between): f(0) = -4 < 0, so y decreases toward -2.
        y(0) = 3 (above 2): y increases without bound (finite-time blow-up).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: equilibrium analysis tells the long-run outcome of a
   model without solving it. In optimization, gradient flow
   d(theta)/dt = -grad L has equilibria at critical points of L: stable
   ones are local minima, unstable ones maxima/saddles.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: confusing stable/unstable; forgetting equilibrium solutions
   when separating variables; assuming every solution converges.
parts.J:
RELATED: gradient-flow equilibria are critical points of the loss
   (F43.2); stability of fixed points of iterations.

G. EXAMPLES
   Linear: y' = -2 (y - 3): equilibrium y* = 3; f' = -2 < 0: stable.
        Solution y = 3 + (y0 - 3) e^(-2t) -> 3 as t -> inf for every y0.
   Logistic: y' = r y (1 - y/K): f(y) = r y (1 - y/K); equilibria 0 and K.
        f'(y) = r (1 - 2y/K): f'(0) = r > 0: UNSTABLE; f'(K) = -r < 0:
        STABLE. Any positive initial population tends to K.
   Moderate: y' = y^2 - 4 = (y - 2)(y + 2): equilibria -2, 2.
        f' = 2y: f'(-2) = -4 < 0 stable; f'(2) = 4 > 0 unstable.
        y(0) = 0 (between): f(0) = -4 < 0, so y decreases toward -2.
        y(0) = 3 (above 2): y increases without bound (finite-time blow-up).
H. INTERPRETATION: equilibrium analysis tells the long-run outcome of a
   model without solving it. In optimization, gradient flow
   d(theta)/dt = -grad L has equilibria at critical points of L: stable
   ones are local minima, unstable ones maxima/saddles.
I. MISTAKES: confusing stable/unstable; forgetting equilibrium solutions
   when separating variables; assuming every solution converges.
J. RELATED: gradient-flow equilibria are critical points of the loss
   (F43.2); stability of fixed points of iterations.

F16.4  EQUILIBRIA OF AUTONOMOUS EQUATIONS y' = f(y)
B. EQUILIBRIUM (constant) solution y = y*: f(y*) = 0.
   STABILITY (linearization): if f'(y*) < 0 the equilibrium is STABLE
   (a sink: nearby solutions approach it); if f'(y*) > 0 it is UNSTABLE
   (a source: solutions move away). If f'(y*) = 0: inconclusive; use the
   sign of f around y*.
   Phase-line rule: y increases where f(y) > 0 and decreases where f(y) < 0.
C. SYMBOLS: y* an equilibrium (f(y*) = 0); f'(y*) the slope of f there
   (stability indicator).
D. CONCEPT: solutions of y' = f(y) never cross (uniqueness), and being
   monotone they either settle to an equilibrium or run off to infinity.
E. CONDITIONS: the equation is autonomous (no explicit t); linearization
   is conclusive when f'(y*) != 0.
G. EXAMPLES
   Linear: y' = -2 (y - 3): equilibrium y* = 3; f' = -2 < 0: stable.
        Solution y = 3 + (y0 - 3) e^(-2t) -> 3 as t -> inf for every y0.

parts.B: FORMULA: y_(n+1) = y_n + h f(t_n, y_n), t_(n+1) = t_n + h.
parts.C: SYMBOLS: h step size.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: follow the tangent line for a short step (F3.2). Error is of
   order h per unit time (first-order method).
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: the global error is of order h (first-order accuracy);
   too large a step h can be unstable (for y' = -ky need h < 2/k).
parts.G:
EXAMPLE: y' = y, y(0) = 1, h = 0.1: y_1 = 1.1, y_2 = 1.21, y_3 = 1.331;
   exact y(0.3) = e^0.3 = 1.34986. Smaller h gives a smaller error.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: a numerical solver advances the solution by repeated
   tangent-line steps; halving h roughly halves the error.
parts.I:

   and global (accumulated) error.
parts.J:
RELATED: gradient descent theta_(n+1) = theta_n - eta grad L(theta_n) IS
   Euler's method for gradient flow with step h = eta.

blocks.title: COMPARISON TABLE: SEPARABLE vs LINEAR FIRST-ORDER ODEs
blocks.rawText:
Aspect           Separable                 Linear first-order
  Form             y' = g(x) h(y)            y' + P(x) y = Q(x)
  Method           separate and integrate    integrating factor
  Linear in y?     not necessarily           must be
  Example          y' = x y, y' = y(1 - y)   y' + 2y = e^(-x)
  Overlap          y' = P(x) y (homogeneous linear) is both
  Pitfall          lost equilibria           forgetting standard form
